articles.title: DOLE says AI not a threat but strategic opportunity
articles.summary: The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Thursday that it is optimistic about artificial intelligence (AI), noting that it is not a threat but an opportunity to be treated responsibly.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 8:32pm
The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Thursday that it is optimistic about artificial intelligence (AI), noting that it is not a threat but an opportunity to be treated responsibly.

“We in the Department of Labor and Employment view AI not as a threat to be feared but as a strategic opportunity to be harnessed responsibly,” said DOLE Monitoring and Evaluation Division chief Hannah Gale Perea during the HR&WorkTech Summit 2026 in Quezon City.
According to the World Economic Forum (WEF), literacy on AI and big data is the number one fastest-growing skill by 2030.

“AI enables our domestic industries to transition towards higher-value services, moving up the global value chain into areas such as AI system oversight, complex analytics, and high-tier technical support,” Perea said.
But in the same report by the WEF, analytical thinking is the top skill needed in the workplace in 2025.
For its part, DOLE said that management of AI exposure in the workplace dictates whether it will result in displacement or employment transformation.
“By augmenting human capability rather than simply replacing it, AI can increase overall productivity, elevate wage potential, and improve working conditions,” said Perea.

The Philippine digital economy reached a Gross Value Added (GVA) of P2.74 trillion in 2025, accounting for 9.8% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) in April.
In 2025, the digital economy employed 10.39 million people, accounting for 21.2% of the country’s total workforce. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
articles.summary: Rescue officials fear more people are buried under the debris in the north-western city of Peshawar.
articles.byline: Bilal Ahmed and Azizullah Khan, Phelan Chatterjee

blocks.text: At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials.
More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Several children are feared to be trapped under the rubble.
Emergency services were alerted to the incident at the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, a rescue official said.
He told the BBC the roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, causing ceilings below to cave in as well.
Warning: This article contains distressing details
"The children in the affected [classrooms] were trapped under the debris," the official, Bilal Faizi, said.
The school is located in a building that had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak.

Earlier reports suggested the affected classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said.
It appears that when the roof of the upper-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too.
Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear.

articles.title: LIVESTREAM: Maria Ressa, WNYC’s Brian Lehrer discuss democracy in the age of AI
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa joins WNYC's Brian Lehrer for a live conversation on defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of artificial intelligence

blocks.text: RESSA. Nobel Peace Prize 2021 laureate and Rappler CEO at the Social Good Summit 2025, in Pasay City on November 16, 2025.
Angie de Silva/Rappler
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa joins WNYC's Brian Lehrer for a live conversation on defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of artificial intelligence

MANILA, Philippines – Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa will join WNYC host Brian Lehrer for a conversation on democracy in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) on Thursday, October 15, in New York (Friday, October 16, Philippine time).
The event, “Democracy Dialogues,” is co-presented by New York Public Radio (NYPR) and Rappler and will take place at The Greene Space in Lower Manhattan.

Lehrer, host of the Peabody Award-winning The Brian Lehrer Show, and Ressa will discuss the challenges of understanding, defending, and rebuilding democracy at a time when AI is rapidly transforming how people access information and engage with the world.
“Democracy Dialogues” is NYPR’s ongoing live event series examining the state of democracy and the roles of journalism, free expression, and an informed public in sustaining democratic institutions.
The conversation comes as Ressa releases her new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, on October 13.

The event will also be livestreamed on WNYC’s website, C-SPAN, and on Rappler’s YouTube channel. Portions of the conversation will air on The Brian Lehrer Show on Friday, October 16, at 10 am Eastern Time.
Watch the livestream starting at 7 am on Friday, October 16 (Philippine time), or 7 pm on Thursday, October 15 (US Eastern Time). – Rappler.com

articles.title: Should you upgrade to the iPhone 18 Pro Max?
articles.summary: After unboxing our early access to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, we were able to make some conclusions. Are you looking for a better camera? If your answer is yes then know that Apple has completely…

blocks.text: After unboxing our early access to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, we were able to make some conclusions.
Are you looking for a better camera?

If your answer is yes then know that Apple has completely re-engineered the main camera of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with a variable aperture. If you zoom in on the main lens you can actually see the opening move to adjust how much light comes in. You can go from the widest f/1.48 for very low light areas to f/4.0 for wider shots.
Are you a professional creative who needs to secure copyright?

If you are a creative professional, Apple has also introduced Reference Image on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Whenever you take a photo, your phone stamps a cryptographic identifier to the photo which is like the equivalent of a digital negative. This is useful in the age of AI and social media where one needs to prove that an image was taken by the original creator and prove copyright.
Are you looking to use this without a case?

Although it may look very similar on the outside, the new Pro and Pro Max have a different layout on the vapor chamber where the A20 chip and RAM are not sandwiched on top of one another, but placed side by side. This allows for better cooling in the vapor chamber. Previous models would heat up by the camera plateau but this has been vastly improved – yes there’s still heat build up but significantly less now. That means you can use the new iPhones with those minimalist case brackets.

blocks.caption: iPhone 18 Pro Max Unit in Silver

blocks.text: That being said, the new iPhone 18 Pro Max has the exact same button configuration as the previous model which means your old cases will work fine!

If money is no object and you’re willing to upgrade anyway, you can always give your old iPhone to your child. That also means that for parents, iOS 27 has completely revamped the parental controls onboarding, making it easier to monitor your kid’s Internet behavior on iOS or iPad OS. Simply reset your old phone, say you’re setting up the iPhone for your child, and follow the on-screen instructions.

blocks.caption: iPhone 18 Pro Max camera module

blocks.text: Other than improved battery life if you find these reasons compelling enough to get you to upgrade, the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are launching at midnight with many store promos from official stores so you don’t get scammed!

Detectives had executed a search warrant at Paporakis’ residence and recovered a rifle, multiple loaded rifle magazines and hundreds of rounds of additional rifle ammunition, police said.
“Among ⁠the recovered items was a tactical vest containing body armor and a patch displaying imagery associated ​with white supremacist extremism,” Palatine police added.

Detectives examined ‌electronic communications and a document attributed ‌to Paporakis – “Why I Fought: A.K.A.: (Aurora Shooter’s Manifesto)” – which had statements expressing white supremacist and extremist ideologies, including ‌references to violence directed toward individuals of South Asian heritage, particularly those of Indian descent.
India’s foreign ministry said it was “deeply concerned” by the incident, and its “anti-Hindu and racist nature” was “particularly disturbing”.
“We expect US authorities to thoroughly investigate the matter, bring those responsible to justice, and take all necessary measures to prevent such incidents,” it said in a statement.
The statement comes days before US secretary ‌of state Marco Rubio’s visit to India, and as long-running efforts to finalize a bilateral trade agreement between the countries have stalled again.
Detectives believe Paporakis may have been ​planning to carry out an attack on 11 October, potentially targeting a Hindu place of worship in Aurora.
“However, the specific intended location has not been confirmed and remains under investigation,” the police said, adding the FBI was assisting in the investigation.
Police said after consultation ⁠with prosecutors from the Cook county state’s attorney’s office, Paporakis faced felony charges of “making ​a terrorist threat” and ​unlawful weapon possession.
The suspect appeared for a ​detention hearing on Wednesday where a judge ordered him detained, according to police, ​who said his next court ‌appearance is scheduled ​for 30 October.

Human ​rights advocates have said that hate against South Asians has spiked in the US in recent years due to factors such as rising anti-immigration rhetoric and policies as well as a rise in white supremacist ideology.

articles.title: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as public water supplies under threat
articles.summary:
Some reservoirs in south-east and south-west at critically low levels as water companies call for non-essential user bans on businesses

A severe drought has been declared in six areas of…

blocks.text: A severe drought has been declared in six areas of England with some reservoirs at critically low levels, threatening public supplies.
Parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex have moved into severe drought, and urgent measures are being taken to secure public supplies of water.

Despite the crisis, the environment secretary Angela Eagle has yet to approve requests from three water companies, in areas now in severe drought, to extend restrictions on water use to businesses such as golf clubs and commercial car washes.
Emma Hardy, the water minister, indicated on Thursday that the environment could suffer in the ongoing drought.

Hardy instructed the Environment Agency to prioritise protecting public water supplies in areas affected by severe drought where there is an unavoidable trade-off between environmental rules and water supplies.
After a meeting of the national drought group, Eagle, said: “This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades, so this government is stepping up our support and planning.
“We are working closely with water companies to protect public supplies in the areas affected, and I’d continue to urge everyone to think about how they can use water wisely over the coming weeks.”

South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water want to impose non-essential user bans on businesses to protect supplies. This would affect golf clubs, private schools and commercial properties. But while Eagle called on water companies to step up their drought planning, she did not announce approval for the non-essential user bans.
The south-east and south-west of England have experienced their driest April to September in more than a century, fuelled by the climate crisis, affecting reservoir levels in those areas.
Levels at two reservoirs are critically low. Ardingly reservoir, which serves about 95,000 properties in Haywards Heath, Uckfield and surrounding areas, is only 19% full.
Storage at Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers in East Devon, North Devon, Somerset and West Dorset and Wessex Water customers in West Somerset, is at 16%.
The Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% for this time of year.

There are also concerns for several smaller South West Water reservoirs serving homes in Devon and Cornwall; these include Drift and Stithians which supply 56,000 households in Cornwall, and the Tottiford and Venford group which supplies 47,000 households in Devon.

The National Drought Group said the government and the Environment Agency would move to daily monitoring of reservoir and river levels and run heightened water quality monitoring because of the lower dilution levels of sewage, raising the risks for water quality and environmental pollution.
Businesses that abstract water will be put through more compliance checks to make sure they are taking only what they are allowed.

Philip Duffy, the chief executive of the EA, said: “We cannot change the weather, but water companies can act now. We expect them to follow their drought plans and take the steps needed to secure public water supplies.
“We are also asking everyone to use less water. That will leave more in our rivers and the environment, helping farmers and protecting wildlife and nature.”

articles.title: Hypersonic missiles highlight arms race on Korean Peninsula
articles.summary: Both South and North Korea have tested weapons feared by military planners for their speed and ability to maneuver in flight.

image.caption: Hypersonic missiles are far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy [FILE: January 6, 2022]Image: YONHAPNEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea announced that it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on Wednesday — a day after the state-run Korean Central News Agency reported that leader Kim Jong Un had visited a new defense industry museum, where he admired an intercontinental ballistic missile reportedly capable of hitting targets in the continental United States.
The visit came five days after South Korean President Lee Jae-myung observed the test launch of his country's first domestically developed hypersonic missile.

South Korea's breakthrough came after Pyongyang announced a test on October 3 of what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that traveled 350 kilometers (220 miles) before striking its target.

"Comrade Kim Jong Un expressed the expectation and belief that all the nation's missile forces would remain faithful to their missions of defending the sovereignty and security of the republic in a responsible combat posture," the KCNA reported.
'Advanced conventional weapons'
Both North and South Korea are primarily racing to develop hypersonic technology because it offers a step-up in offensive capabilities at a time of worsening tensions in the Indo-Pacific region.

blocks.caption: Pyongyang said it had tested two types of submarine-launched cruise missiles off its east coast on October 14Image: KCNA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Hypersonic missiles are weapons that can travel at velocities of at least five times the speed of sound (Mach 5) or over 6,100 kilometers per hour.

Their speed makes it far harder for defenders to identify, track and destroy inbound missiles, which can carry conventional or nuclear warheads. Their additional advantage over previous generations of missiles is their ability to suddenly change course, dip or weave in flight, making interception significantly more difficult.

"There has been an arms race on the Korean Peninsula for many years and hypersonic weapons are just the latest manifestation of that," said Chris Green, Korea Peninsula analyst for Crisis Group International.
Hypersonic weapons have become a "priority for the South" as the North has ramped up its capabilities and forged military and economic ties with Russia, he said.
"And North Korea has nuclear weapons, but it would not be viable to use them as the threat has always been that doing so would mean that the US would turn the country to glass," he told DW.
"For the North, it is unsurprising that the geopolitics of the region have encouraged them to pursue advanced conventional weapons as they try to have dominance on the peninsula."
What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war?
Pyongyang 'should not be underestimated'

And while it is impossible to confirm with any certainty that the weapons the North says it has developed have the capabilities they claim, Green said it would be a mistake to underestimate Pyongyang.

"We do not know their capabilities and it is possible this is all propaganda, but there is a long list of times the North's capabilities have been underestimated only to be shown that they can, in fact, do what they say."
Chun In-bum, a retired general in the South Korean army and now a senior fellow with the National Institute for Deterrence Studies, shares that assessment of the threat.
"It's anybody's guess whether they're telling the truth on this, but any prudent military planner should always assume the worst," he said.
The North's mastery of the advanced technology required to operate hypersonic missiles appears to have been sudden, although it remains unclear how it acquired the capability.

"They probably obtained the technology through illegal means," Chun said. "They snoop around firms in the US, South Korea and Japan for this sort of information, but they also do it to their 'friends.'"
Wherever the data came from, the fact that North Korea's hypersonic missiles appear to have performed as required should be cause for deep concern.

"A greater offensive capability increases the overall danger posed by the North, and if they have weapons that are harder to shoot down, then it is possible there are greater temptations to use them," Chun said.
"I'm speculating, of course, but I'm sure that we are looking at ways to neutralize this particular threat, but as I understand it there is no good answer right now," Chun added.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
Canceling each other out?
Green, however, believes that both sides developing viable systems means that they may cancel each other out as a potent battlefield advantage.

"I do not think this changes the balance of power," he said. "The North still has its nuclear deterrent and this 'porcupine strategy' of being sharp and prickly in order to keep everyone else at arm's length. And it's not a game changer south of the Demilitarized Zone either," the expert added.

"It is clear, however, that if the North continues to develop its offensive systems and is able to deploy them in huge numbers, then there will have to be a conversation about greater missile defense not only in the South but also in Japan, and that will then raise some very difficult questions."

articles.title: Bad news for Trump ahead of the midterms: it’s still the economy, stupid
articles.summary: Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect

blocks.text: It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections.

In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse. About six months later, as Donald Trump launched a trade war on the rest of the world with his “liberation day” tariffs, the share of Republican pessimists had dropped to 33%.

It’s hard to detect a reason for this in the economic data. Annual consumer price inflation fell from 2.4% to 2.3% between the two polls. The unemployment rate ticked up from 4.1% to 4.2%. Indeed, Democrats disagreed sharply with their Republican neighbors: from the last Harris poll of the Biden era to the first under Trump, the share who thought the US economy was worsening jumped from 28% to 73%.

As the midterm elections loom into focus, suggesting a stark Republican defeat, Trump and his minions are hoping that this ideological lens, shaping economic reality to fit political preferences, can prevent an electoral bloodbath in November. Maybe Trump can somehow dupe the Maga base into believing that “we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before.”

From three weeks out, it seems pretty clear that the gambit is not going to work. Polling by Harris for the Guardian suggests that the economy is looking pretty bad even for their most loyal acolytes. Too bad to convince them otherwise.

The September reading of the consumer price index, which recorded a spike in annual inflation to 3.7%, had not yet been published when Harris performed its latest round of polling earlier this month. Still, the pollster reported that 38% of Republicans believe the economy is worsening. That is up from 29% a year ago.

The pattern is evident among cohorts that have proven historical Republican bulwarks. Rural Americans, loyal Republican allies for decades, are being battered by Trump’s policies. They were hit not only by his trade war, largely barred from China’s markets. They have been hammered by the rising price of diesel and fertilizer, for which they can thank Trump’s war in Iran. They have been hamstrung by Trump’s raids against the many immigrants in their labor force. And they feel roundly attacked by Trump’s attempt to tame rising beef prices by lowering tariffs on imported meat.

Unsurprisingly, this is showing up in the polling. Sixty-four percent of rural Americans polled this month said the economy was getting worse, compared to only 52% of city dwellers. Six percent more rural residents think the economy is worsening than in September 2024, during the last poll of the Biden administration. White Americans, another pillar of Republican support, are also turning sour: 61% believe the economy is getting worse, up from 48% in September of 2024. The share of men who believe the economy is getting worse increased from 46% to 52% over those two years.

Bill Clinton famously won the presidency in 1992 campaigning on: “It’s the economy, stupid.” For much of the 20th century the state of the economy was critical in deciding presidential and congressional elections. Voters blamed or rewarded incumbents for the state of the economy. The relationship was always moderated by partisan preferences, though. And it has weakened dramatically as the electorate has set on divergent ideological paths, ultimately splitting into rival camps with diametrically opposed perceptions of reality.

“The economic perceptions of Democrats and Republicans have polarized relative to Independents and that this polarization is not asymmetric in magnitude,” argued a recent study by political scientists from Stanford and New York University. They estimate the partisan gap in economic perceptions rose “from about 20 percentage-points at the beginning of the Bush II administration to a maximum of 73 percentage-points during the (first) Trump administration”.
after newsletter promotion

Partisanship doesn’t just affect voters’ perceptions of the economy. As reported by political scientists at Bucknell University and Texas A&M University, polarization reduces policymakers’ incentive to tailor policy to deliver broad economic prosperity.

“If voters are relatively unwilling to cross party lines to reward good economic performance or punish economic decline, then elected officials can pursue policies that distribute economic benefits narrowly without affecting their chances of re-election,” they wrote. “This might include aiming policy to deliver rewards to co-partisans, donors, or even to the office-holder himself or herself.”

This would explain Trump’s tactics to a T. Not only has he taken to scaring voters with culture war stuff – variously branding Democrats as apologists of Vladimir Lenin and claiming that they want to change the sex of young children. He seems to believe that he can sway the electorate by doing violence to groups that his Maga base dislikes, like immigrants and the “undeserving” poor. Maybe they will pay less attention to the cost of living, and to the Trump family’s self-dealing.

It seems too late, though. Voters’ opposition to Trump’s economic stewardship is too well established, having built up since the “liberation day” tariffs through countless destructive decisions over the last 21 months. He has not only lost average US voters – 58% of those think the economy is getting worse, 10 percentage points more than in the last poll of the Biden era. His shots at distracting the base are unlikely to convince them that they are not, in fact, miserable too.

articles.title: John Healey vows to give ‘breathing space’ to consumers and businesses in first budget
articles.summary: Speaking at IMF meeting, chancellor says he will stick to fiscal rules while recognising business and living costs

blocks.text: John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules.
Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs.

“I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space – but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future,” he said.

The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills, but Healey is expected to announce a further package of energy support at his 28 October tax and spending statement, before what is expected to be a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January.
He said: “The prime minister’s talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living.”

Healey also reiterated his insistence that he would be sticking to the spending plans set out by his predecessor Rachel Reeves at last year’s spending review – and that cabinet colleagues would have to find any additional resources within their existing budgets.

“When the second half of a spending review is in place, there are pressures on departments, and colleagues are doing a good job of managing with what they’ve got,” he said, adding: “You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things.”
The UK has been praised by the IMF this week for setting out a plan to tackle its deficit, with the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urging the government to “stay the course”.

Healey stressed he would stick to the rules set out by Reeves. “We will meet those fiscal rules, and I think one of the hallmarks of the IMF’s backing of our fiscal plans is recognition that there isn’t just a forecast for the future, but there’s some evidence of performance already.”
He declined to say whether he would increase taxes on banks, or raise capital gains tax, to offset the expected pressure on his budget from higher energy prices and government borrowing costs.

“If you think back to the run-up to previous budgets, the speculation about what was set to be in those budgets was actually deeply damaging,” he said. “It led to people cashing in their pensions early when they didn’t need to. It led to people holding back or not investing in their businesses when they didn’t need to. So I’m just not going to get drawn into any speculation.”
after newsletter promotion
Healey, a former defence secretary, also hinted he was working on an additional package of support for Ukraine, to be announced at the budget.

He said: “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine: military, diplomatic and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with [Vladimir] Putin targeting these energy systems with thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching.
“The step back from this is that the future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.”
Healey and the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, chaired a meeting of G20 policymakers on Thursday morning, in the absence of the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent.
The chancellor will fly back to London on Thursday evening to put the finishing touches to the budget.

items: What is the likely impact of the loss of Starlink? blocks.text: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry

blocks.caption: The international criminal court is investigating allegations of war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA

articles.title: PCG fends off Chinese vessel, 4 small boats off Lawak Island in Palawan
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Thursday (Oct. 15) chased off a Chinese fishing vessel and four small boats within the territorial waters of Lawak Island, west of Palawan.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) on Thursday (Oct. 15) chased off a Chinese fishing vessel and four small boats within the territorial waters of Lawak Island, west of Palawan.
According to the PCG, the Chinese fishing vessel (CFV) Yuetaiyu 63168 was anchored off the island’s territorial waters.
Lawak Island is part of the municipality of Kalayaan in Palawan province.
The PCG noted that, under international laws, the country exercises full sovereignty over its territorial seas, “where no foreign vessel may fish without authorization.”
It deployed a team aboard a rubber boat to the vessel’s location, where it discovered four small boats scattered in the vicinity.
Passengers in the foreign boats were observed to be engaging in fishing.
The PCG personnel issued several radio calls to the Chinese fishing vessel, while circling it three times, but received no response.
It then proceeded to drive away the four small boats.
“The PCG team did not leave the area until the Chinese fishing vessel heaved in its anchor and departed,” PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said in a statement.
The small boats also retreated back to its mother vessel.
“The PCG team returned to Lawak Island without any untoward incident,” Tarriela said.

The incident follows the PCG’s earlier operations in Kalayaan Island Group (KIG), where it also repelled Chinese Maritime Militia Vessel 9622 and its 24 small boats (sampans) off Kota Island last Sept. 28.
It also drove away the same vessel with 22 sampans near the island on Oct. 9, reportedly fishing and dumping waste at sea.
Five unauthorized foreign fishing vessels were also monitored in the same area on Oct. 11, the PCG added.

“The deployment of small boats from a Chinese mother vessel to conduct fishing activities in these waters is a violation of Philippine laws, including the Philippine Fisheries Code and the Philippine Maritime Zones Act,” Tarriela stressed.
The PCG continues to monitor Chinese fishing vessel Yuetaiyu for any possible further movements.
It added that its surveillance in the KIG against unauthorized fishing or intrusions of foreign vessels will go on. /apl

articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries as Zelenskyy says 'we're done'
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that Ukraine is resuming attacks on Russian energy sites. It came after Moscow summarily ignored a claim by US President Donald Trump that an "energy ceasefire" had…

image.caption: Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian refineries after Russia fails to observe US 'truce'Image: EyePress News/Newscom/IMAGO

blocks.text: Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Thursday said that his country's military had resumed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.
Zelenskyy made the statement in an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, saying: "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out. We're done."
The announcement came after Russia reported Ukrainian attacks on oil processing plants in Ryazan, where fire broke out, and Saratov.
Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.

On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.

blocks.caption: Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Trump's 'ceasefire' on energy sites: 'We're done'Image: Dan Bashakov/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kyiv's blasts dangerous lack of US intel
Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.

To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."
Ukraine: Russian strikes continue as ceasefire questions remain
Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.
"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.

Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.
Zelenskyy: Starlink throttling a question of US 'will'
Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."
SpaceX owner Elon Musk said the US owns and operates the Starshield military version of Starlink used by Ukraine, adding that he and his company had nothing to do with the issue.
Ukraine presses allies on intelligence sharing

The FT interview comes in the wake of Trump's decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil as well as his promise to buy "millions of barrels" of Russian diesel fuel amid high fuel prices caused by the US war with Iran.

The deal, just weeks from the US midterm elections, is unlikely to bring down oil prices. But it does extend a lifeline to Russian President Putin, allowing him to continue his illegal invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy and went so far as to call for him to be replaced this weekend.
Trump's sanctions actions fly in the face of nearly five years of allied political efforts to pressure Moscow to end its invasion.
Trump's actions have enraged NATO allies and European leaders, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, for one, calling the US agreement to purchase Russian diesel "a very risky decision."

Meloni pointed out that the spike in oil prices was clearly precipitated by Trump's war in Iran and that his dealings with Putin would result in the Russian leader continuing his invasion of Ukraine rather than ending it.

articles.title: Romania: 2 ships on fire in Black Sea, 7 crew missing
articles.summary: Two chemical tankers have caught fire in Romanian territorial waters in the Black Sea. The blazes occurred after Russian drones were sighted in Romanian airspace.

image.caption: Several crew members from the Wine Trader are missing after a fire broke out onboardImage: Romanian Interior Ministry/REUTERS

blocks.text: Romanian authorities have launched search and rescue operations in the Black Sea in a bid to find seven missing crew from a chemical tanker that caught fire overnight to Thursday.
Another vessel, also a chemical tanker, was also set on fire in the same region some hours earlier, but all its crew is said to be safe.
The fires occurred after Russian drones strayed into Romanian airspace, though Romanian officials have so far not explicitly said the unmanned aircraft caused the blazes.

However, there have been drone strikes on at least five other cargo ships off the coasts of Romanian and neighboring Bulgaria — both NATO members — in the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors lost in those incidents.
What do we know about the ship fires in the Black Sea?
Both ships were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina Canal leading ‌to the Black Sea out of the Danube River when they caught fire.
Romania's naval authority said it launched its search and rescue operation after receiving an emergency alert ‌from ​the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader.
Five of the 12 crew members were said to be safe, while seven were missing.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," Defense Minister Radu Miruta told the Digi24 television channel.
"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.
The other fire, which broke out earlier, occurred onboard the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J.
Ships often use the canal as a place to anchor in the case of delays caused by weather or congestion.
Growing attacks in the Black Sea

Romania, which shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, has ⁠reported ​repeated breaches of its airspace by Russian drones over ​the past four years during Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.
The Danube and its ports are now frequently used by Ukrainian vessels as Ukraine's Black Sea ports come under attack from Russian forces.
Ukrainian ships are also choosing routes in the Black Sea close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
This comes as shipping in the Black Sea has come under increasing attacks ​⁠in recent months that have drastically reduced grain transports from both Ukraine and Russia, both major cereal exporters.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Thursday that the EU, of which both his country and Romania are members, will discuss a proposed moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea at its ongoing summit in Brussels.
Bulgaria summoned the Russian ambassador over the sinking of a ship off the country's coast on Tuesday following a drone attack.

articles.title: UP Diliman students evacuate 2 school buildings after alleged threat
articles.summary: Students, faculty, and staff at two school buildings in the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman campus in Quezon City were evacuated Thursday afternoon due to an alleged security threat.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 7:22pm
Students, faculty, and staff at two school buildings in the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman campus in Quezon City were evacuated Thursday afternoon due to an alleged security threat.
According to a report by Tinig ng Plaridel, the student publication in UP Diliman College of Mass Communication, evacuation measures were implemented at Palma Hall and Malcolm Hall.
Images posted by Tinig ng Plaridel showed police responders clad in black combat gear speaking with a security guard on the Palma Hall steps.
A vehicle of the Quezon City (QC) Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (DRRMO) was parked nearby as students walked down the stairs.

The report quoted the UP Office of the Vice Chancellor for Community Affairs (OVCCA) as confirming the presence of personnel from QC DRRMO and the QC Police District's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit to investigate the incident.
Youscooper Dawson Quiambao documented the exit of students at Palma Hall past 2 p.m.
According to a report by Isa Avendano-Umali on Super Radyo dzBB, a threat was posted on social media, which stated: "Maghahasik ng lagim sa buong Palma at Malcolm. Humanda kayong lahat."
(Horror will be unleashed all over Palma and Malcom. All of you be ready.)
Palma Hall, also known the College of Social Sciences and Philosophy (CSSP), is a major convergence point in the UP Diliman campus as courses of various disciplines are taught there.
On the other hand, Malcolm Hall is the UP College of Law.
The radio report added that the QCPD Explosive Ordnance Disposal team and school officials immediately responded by initiating inspections and safety procedures.
Authorities did not find any suspicious or hazardous items, the report said.
The QCPD was quoted as saying that investigation was still ongoing. The situation in the two buildings went back to normal as of posting time.

GMA News Online's calls to OVCCA phone numbers were unanswered. GMA News Online likewise reached out to the QC DRRMO but it has yet to respond as of this post. For its part, the QCPD said it would issue a statement at a later time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
articles.summary: A search and rescue operation is under way in the Black Sea after the latest attack in the area.

blocks.text: Eight of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a tanker ablaze off Romania's coast, naval authorities say.

The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire on Thursday morning. Romanian President Nicușor Dan later confirmed it was struck by drones.
The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. A swarm of Russian drones were detected overnight not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island.
Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port were hit during the sea crossing. It did not name the vessels.
On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy.
A search and rescue operation for the eight missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed.
The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel.
The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area.
The tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT).
Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader was hit by two drones.
The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked.
This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened.
The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state."
Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region.
The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area.
Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports.
On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable".
Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi.
Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports.
Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Refinery owned by Russian oil giant Rosneft hit with Ukraine drone attack

Ukraine has resumed ‌its attacks on Russian refineries with a strike at an installation in the Ryazan region, the regional governor said Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his anger at the withdrawal of U.S. intelligence.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump's surprise announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had ​refrained from attacking Russian refineries, which the U.S. leader had blamed for ​raising diesel prices on global markets.

But Zelenskyy had voiced increasing frustration with Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, which on Wednesday had left 600,000 people without power, he said. He warned that ​Ukraine would not suspend its own attacks indefinitely if Russia did not reciprocate and also criticized what ⁠he said was Trump's favouritism ⁠toward Russia.
In an interview with the Financial Times published ‌on Thursday, he said Ukraine's patience had run out. "The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We're done."

items: Starlink restrictions may hamper Ukraine's war effort. But the country can adapt, experts say
12 U.S. senators, including 6 Republicans, tell Trump to drop diesel deal with Russia

blocks.text: Pavel Malkov, the governor of Russia's Ryazan region, said in a post on Telegram that a major Ukrainian drone attack on the area had sparked a fire at an oil refinery.
"The material damage is now being ⁠assessed. Emergency services are working at the scene," he said.

The Ryazan refinery is owned by Russian oil giant Rosneft and feeds Moscow with fuel. It has been attacked several times by drones in recent months. The refinery accounts for almost five per cent of Russia's total oil refining throughput.
The Current19:20Is President Trump’s diesel deal reshaping the Ukraine war?
No European alternative to Starlink
In his interview, Zelenskyy criticized Washington's eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and Trump's apparent admiration for Russia's Vladimir Putin.

Trump on Saturday called for Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy and railed against Ukraine's attacks on ‌Russian oil infrastructure, one day after announcing a diesel supply deal with Russia, aiming to lower fuel prices that have soared since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are disrupting military operations

Despite Ukraine's suspension of refinery attacks for three days, Ukrainian officials complained that they had not received any U.S. early-warning alerts in recent days for incoming Russian ballistic missiles.

They also ​said the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications service had been slowed across the country, hampering front-line operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military sites.
Musk said Wednesday in a post on X that Starshield — the military version of Starlink — was owned and controlled by the U.S. ⁠government, which decided on any limits on speed.

items: Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign

blocks.text: Zelenskyy has said that Ukrainian military officials were warned by their U.S. ⁠counterparts ⁠that Washington would block intelligence unless they halted ​strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
In the FT interview, Zelenskyy said the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but he ​dismissed that possibility, calling it a matter of "will."
Europe does not have a ready-made alternative to Starlink that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.

Asked whether Ukraine would be open to halting energy strikes as a way of repairing relations with the White House, Zelenskyy told the newspaper he could only agree if in return he was given more U.S.-made Patriot interceptors, calling it the "minimum" that would be ⁠acceptable.

Trump has had a contentious relationship with Ukraine's president, dating back to 2019 when he was impeached by the Democrat-led U.S. House of Representatives for pressuring Zelenskyy for a political favour in exchange for military aid for Ukraine. Trump was acquitted in the U.S. Senate.
Trump has also been highly critical of the amount of military and humanitarian aid given to Ukraine by Joe Biden's presidential administration after Russia's 2022 invasion.
3 killed in central Ukraine
Ukraine's ⁠air ​force said 580 Russian drones ​attacked ⁠the country overnight, with 536 shot down.

The central Ukrainian region of Kirovohrad was hit ‌by the largest Russian attack on its territory during ​the war, killing ​three people and wounding another six overnight, ​the local governor ⁠said Thursday.
Firefighters work at the site of an enterprise hit by a Russian drone strike on Thursday in Kropyvnytskyi. (State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Reuters)
The region, a relatively infrequent target of bombardment, was hit by ⁠more than 360 drones, local governor Andriy Raikovych wrote ‌on Telegram.
"The enemy ​deliberately hit critical ⁠infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities ⁠and residential homes," he ⁠wrote.
Russia also hit Ukraine's ‌Naftogaz gas-extraction ​facility in the ​central Poltava region ​overnight, ⁠the company ⁠said.
It said in ⁠a statement on Telegram that the ​attack suspended ⁠the ⁠operations, ⁠damaged ⁠equipment and ​caused a ​fire.

Ukraine's military said Thursday it had damaged six Russian Su-34M military aircraft in an overnight strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield in Russia's Voronezh region. The Su-34M is a large fighter-bomber, costing tens of millions of dollars apiece and frequently used by Russia to drop devastating glide bombs onto Ukrainian cities near the front line.
Reuters could not independently verify the battlefield reports.

articles.title: Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Aleksandar Vučić personally intervened to push plans for controversial $500m Trump Tower in Belgrade, which sparked protests and a criminal case

Serbia’s authoritarian ruler…

blocks.text: Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.

Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.

The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.

The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.

blocks.caption: Jared Kusher and the Serbian president, Aleksandar Vučić, in Belgrade. Photograph: Instagram/Aleksandar Vucic

blocks.text: A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.

After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.

blocks.caption: Screenshot from Trumpbelgrade.com showing the renderings of the proposed Belgrade development. Photograph: Trumpbelgrade.com

blocks.text: “We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”

Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.

Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.

Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.
A free 99-year lease

On 6 February 2024, Dubravka Đukanović, a Serbian conservation professor in her 60s, arrived for a meeting at the presidency, a domed former royal palace. For three years, she had been the director of the country’s institute for the protection of cultural monuments.

The topic was the General Staff building, the former Yugoslav ministry of defence in central Belgrade. The building, an architectural gem seen as an emblem of resistance to the Nazis, was already cherished when Nato forces bombed it in 1999 during its campaign to force Milošević to withdraw from Kosovo, deepening its resonance.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vučić and Donald Trump Jr in Belgrade. Photograph: Facebook/Aleksandar Vucic

blocks.text: Vučić himself had reaffirmed the General Staff building’s legally protected status in 2016. Now, the president said he wanted Đukanović to rescind it, according to two people with knowledge of the meeting. Some unspecified “foreign investor” was keen on the site.

Under Serbian law, stripping the General Staff building of its protected status was not in Đukanović’s gift. Her institute would have to commission an expert opinion, which would have to conclude that there were good reasons why protected status was no longer merited.

But the president wanted it done. At 6ft 6in and intolerant of dissent, Vučić can be intimidating. His tone towards Đukanović and another heritage official present was unpleasant, the sources said. He told them they were lazy and incompetent. The message was clear: do what I want or resign.
A plausible explanation for Vučić’s forceful intervention came the following month, when an agreement between the Serbian government and Kushner’s real estate company leaked.

Married to Trump’s daughter Ivanka, Kushner had been an influential White House aide during his father-in-law’s first term. Since Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election, Kushner had been concentrating on his investment fund.

By early 2024, Trump was storming to the Republican nomination and was favourite to win the coming election. If Trump took back the White House, Kushner would once more be one of the most influential people on the planet.
The leaked agreement showed the Serbian authorities had granted Kushner’s company a 99-year lease over the General Staff site, free of charge.
Kushner, whose spokesperson said he had been looking at the project since 2021, posted an image of the design on X, professing himself “excited”.
Allow content provided by a third party?

This article includes content hosted on platform.x.com. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The news was not universally welcomed in Belgrade. “Serbia is not a buffet, and Vučić is not a waiter,” said Aleksandar Jovanović Ćuta, an environmental activist who revealed the agreement. “This is not his private property.”

Yet Vučić’s regime proceeded to sign a contract, dated 13 May 2024 and seen by the Guardian, undertaking that the “cultural heritage designation” of the site would be removed “to the satisfaction” of Kushner’s company.
Comply or resign
The week after the contract was signed, Đukanović was summoned to another meeting. The president was not there this time. Siniša Mali, his finance minister and right-hand man, took charge.

Mali urged Đukanović and Olivera Vučković, Belgrade’s top heritage official, to cancel the General Staff site’s protected status, according to the indictment’s summary of testimony the two women would later give prosecutors. It makes no reference to the earlier meeting with the president but indicates that the subject had previously been broached.
“Mali asked them if they had given it any thought,” the indictment says, “and if they would initiate the procedure to remove the building’s protected status.”
The women refused, “believing that the legal conditions for it were not met”. In that case, Mali told them, repeating his boss’s ultimatum from February, they should resign. They did.

In her resignation letter, which the Guardian has seen, Đukanović wrote that she could not agree “to inappropriate interventions that would permanently destroy all the values of the complex, which testifies to the highest achievements of contemporary Serbian architecture and is of incalculable importance for preserving enduring creative values, the education of future generations, and the strengthening of the cultural identity of the Serbian people”.

Approached by the Guardian, Đukanović and Vučković confirmed the accuracy of this account. Đukanović added: “I prefer not to make any statement on this matter while the court proceedings are ongoing.”

Little was heard of the General Staff plan for months. In November, Trump beat Kamala Harris to win re-election. Ten days later, Vučić’s government announced that the General Staff site had been stripped of its protected status.
Keeping it in the family

One of the first things Trump did upon regaining the presidency was to ditch the pledge he made in his first term that his family business would refrain from doing deals abroad while he was in office.

“The scale of corruption will be orders of magnitude greater than what we saw in the first Trump administration,” Kathleen Clark, a government ethics lawyer at Washington University School of Law, warned at the time. Trump had made it much easier, she said, to buy his favour.

The family business remained officially under the control of his two oldest sons, Don Jr and Eric. In January 2025, four days after their father’s inauguration, Eric spoke about some new projects. The Trumps and the Kushners, New York real estate families united by marriage, had decided to embark on their first venture together: Kushner’s Belgrade hotel and tower would bear the Trump name.

“It’s going to be fun to bring the family together,” Eric told the New York Times. “Serbia is one of the fastest-growing countries in Europe, and we’re incredibly honoured to be there.” Kushner, who had travelled to Belgrade for what Vučić called an “inspiring” meeting with the Serbian leader, added: “Our research showed that the Trump brand would be the best for this market.”
That brand has enjoyed a surge in demand around the world during Trump’s second term, accompanied by allegations that it comes with a quid pro quo.

blocks.caption: Jared Kushner joins Donald Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, at the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Vietnam, Eric was showered with confetti at the groundbreaking ceremony for a £1.5bn golf resort, the permits for which were granted with unusual speed. Then Trump halved Vietnam’s tariffs. The Saudis poured money into Kushner’s fund, and plans emerged for a Trump plaza in Jeddah. Then Trump agreed to sell the kingdom new US fighter jets. A cryptocurrency baron’s company and senior Emiratis cut a lucrative transaction with World Liberty Financial, the digital currency venture Don Jr and Eric founded. Trump gave the crypto baron a pardon and the Emiratis access to restricted US chips.

Asked about such deals last year, Kushner, now a presidential envoy to Russia, Israel and elsewhere, said: “What people call conflicts of interests … I call experience and trusted relationships that we have throughout the world.”

Those who strike up “trusted relationships” with the Trumps, even if there is not an obvious quid pro quo, gain something less tangible but maybe still more valuable: the aura of friendship with a president who is happy to wield his superpower to make or break smaller nations and their leaders.

Vučić has plenty in common with Trump. Both are friendly with Vladimir Putin and contemptuous of the EU – in Vučić’s case, despite his country having applied to join. A shared disdain for Nato may help explain why the one part of the General Staff building’s heritage that the redevelopment pledged to retain was a memorial to the alliance’s “aggression” against Serbia.
And there is a lot that Vučić could use US help with, not least the fate of Kosovo, which he says is still part of Serbia.

Not long after his father returned to office, Don Jr landed in Belgrade. Vučić said that during their meeting he “emphasised the importance of the economic and political relations between Serbia and the USA and stressed the importance of strategic cooperation between the two countries and joint projects in the years to come”. When Don Jr returned the following month, Vučić fed him a choice sucking-pig.
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

For Vučić, the support of the first family was timely. Days before his regime stripped the General Staff site of its protection, the collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, triggered rolling protests against graft. The student organisers’ slogan has become “Serbia or mafia”.

Don Jr’s visit came on the eve of the biggest demonstration in Serbia’s history. He invited Vučić on to his podcast, Triggered, and declared that the Serb ruler’s opponents were “weaponising” the Novi Sad disaster, just as Trump’s had done with the Capitol riots after his 2020 election defeat.

But the protesters maintained their momentum, and began to rally against the Trump tower. In May 2025, Vučić went to the US, hoping to visit Trump at Mar-a-Lago, his Florida members’ club. He got to see Rudy Giuliani, Trump’s disgraced lawyer, but not the president. State media reported this was because Vučić fell ill.

No sooner was Vučić home than police arrested Goran Vasić, the man who had been installed as head of the heritage institute to replace Dubravka Đukanović following her resignation. To achieve the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protected status, prosecutors said, Vasic had forged a supportive expert opinion.

More arrests followed. In December 2025, Vučić’s culture minister was indicted for abuse of office for his alleged part in the General Staff scheme. Within days, Kushner’s company announced the project was off.
Coup or cover-up?
Vučić’s threat of reprisals was not idle.

His allies attacked Đukanović, claiming that she had tried to profit personally from her time as a heritage official. Her deputy, who received a visit from the state security service after she went on television to denounce the cancellation of the General Staff building’s protection, has been accused of unrelated misconduct. The Serbian conservators’ industry body said this had “the obvious aim of discrediting her”. Both are expected to give evidence in the criminal proceedings.
For the specialist unit of organised-crime prosecutors who brought the charges, this is a watershed case. Never before has a serving Serbian minister been indicted.

Vučić accuses the prosecutors of staging a coup. Others, though, fear they are pulling their punches. That concern increased when Nikola Selaković, the indicted culture minister, used a court appearance in April to reveal that, while police were raiding his ministry, he was in his office sipping plum brandy and smoking cigarettes with Mladen Nenadić, the head of the organised-crime prosecutors’ unit. The unit’s spokesperson said there was “no discussion regarding the course of the case”.
“In everything that happened regarding potential investments, I saw a chance for our country and citizens,” said Selaković, who faces three years in prison if convicted.
Vučić has not been charged. Neither has his lieutenant, Mali. Both deny wrongdoing.

blocks.caption: Aleksandar Vučić addresses the 81st UN general assembly in September. Photograph: Eduardo Muñoz/Reuters

blocks.text: The indictment refers to evidence from witnesses who were present at the Vučić meeting in February 2024 but does not mention it, raising questions about the apparent decision to omit what would appear to be a key part of the narrative.

The spokesperson for the organised crime prosecutors’ unit said that it had evidence regarding Vučić’s February 2024 meeting with the heritage officials. Beyond those already indicted, prosecutors were “conducting pretrial proceedings in this case to determine potential criminal liability of other persons as well”, the spokesperson added.

Vučić has stepped down and cannot seek another term but is expected to retain his control over the regime if he is elected prime minister on 25 October. In one of his last acts as president, he issued 49 pardons. Some of the recipients have not been identified and it is not clear whether they include defendants in the General Staff case.

The White House referred questions to the Trumps’ company. Its representative said: “The Trump Organization has no plans to develop any project in Belgrade, was never, at any point, involved in any discussions or negotiations to acquire any site in Belgrade and denies any involvement in or knowledge of the alleged claims.”

Kushner’s spokesperson said: “The suggestion that Jared Kushner pursued the Belgrade project as part of any political arrangement or ‘pay to play’ scheme is categorically false.” Rather, it was “an opportunity to transform a site associated with a painful chapter in Serbia’s history into a symbol of healing and reconciliation, while bringing substantial private investment, jobs and economic opportunity to Belgrade”.
The spokesperson added: “Jared had no involvement in the Serbian government’s internal processes concerning the site’s protected status.”

For all Vučić’s difficulties, the tale of the Trump Tower Belgrade does not appear to have put others off doing business with the first family. Trump retains stakes in dozens of his companies, even if his sons nominally run them. In July, he released his financial disclosure for his first year back at the White House. It showed he had made $2bn.

articles.title: Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
articles.summary: More than 12,000 people filled a major venue in the city to hear the former US president's take on the challenges the world is facing. .

blocks.text: Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope
But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups.
He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill".
"It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said.
"So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that."
But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable".

He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler.
"We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'."
"We have not chosen to do that."

Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice.
The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make.
He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet."
He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible.
"I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said.
Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted.
"We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people – immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays – that's just talk, it's humour'."
He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant.
Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for.
