articles.title: Thousands of German gamblers could sue for their money back
articles.summary: German gamblers may finally be able to beat the house, thanks to new court rulings in the EU and a federal court. The decisions could help gambling addicts — but the legal road might be difficult.

image.caption: Online gambling is considered much more addictiveImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A German court has followed the European Court of Justice in finding that gamblers can seek compensation from gambling companies if they lost money when online casinos and fruit machines were illegal in Germany.
The verdicts could have major consequences for gambling addicts, as thousands of people could potentially bring civil lawsuits against gambling companies.

A series of court decisions at regional, federal, and European level have found in favor of gamblers in the last year, beginning with the Higher Regional Court Stuttgart in September 2025, which agreed with a plaintiff in the state of Baden-Württemberg who sued the Malta-based online betting company Tipico Games.

The plaintiff lost around €10,000 ($11,200) between 2020 and 2022, but because online gambling was prohibited in Germany until 2021, the court found that operators had therefore received the winnings without legal basis and must return them.
Wins for the losers

Tipico Games then appealed to the Federal Court of Justice (BGH), the highest civil and criminal court in Germany. In an initial verbal hearing in mid-September this year, the court followed the principle of the plaintiffs' case on one key point: That gamblers have the right to claim back losses if the companies did not have a license in Germany at the time the losses were incurred. But a final decision on the case is only expected to be made in January next year.
Online casinos and fruit machines were banned in Germany from 2008 to 2021, but several gambling operators were active in the country because they had gaming licenses in other EU countries.
What online gambling companies don't want you to know

In April this year, the European Court of Justice ruled that EU law does not preclude a member state from "prohibiting certain services," or from "attaching civil-law consequences to that prohibition." In other words, even if a gambling company has a legitimate license in one member state, that doesn't override national gambling laws elsewhere.

Thomas Dünchheim, a business lawyer at global law firm Greenberg Traurig who specializes in gambling law, said law firms were now gathering clients — sometimes trawling the internet with the help of AI tools — to prepare massive collective lawsuits. Dünchheim himself has people who have lost tens of thousands of euros come to him seeking representation.

"The pendulum is swinging more and more towards the consumer. It's a bit like in America — we're seeing a mass phenomenon like the Dieselgate lawsuits against VW," he told DW. "And there are lawyers who will collect all these little cases, bundle them, and then maybe even drive it forward with the help of a legal financing firm. It's a good business for all involved, and the ones that will have to pay are the gambling firms who operated unlawful gambling in Germany."
The dangers of online gambling

The decisions could bring a measure of help for addicts, as online gambling can be particularly dangerous for people with addiction issues. According to Tobias Hayer, a psychologist at the Institute for Public Health and Nursing Research at Bremen University, that comes down to four main features of online gambling: Anonymity and the consequent lack of social control, 24/7 accessibility, the frictionless nature of cashless transactions, and the high frequency of games played.

"These court verdicts are not surprising at all," Hayer told DW, but he added that he had an ambivalent attitude to them. "On the one hand I can imagine that this will be a huge relief to many gamblers who had an addiction problem. On the other hand, if these people suddenly get a lot of money in their hands, but they haven't worked through their problems, then of course there's a danger of recidivism."
Hooked on Gambling
The legal obstacles

But Dünchheim suggested that the gamblers may not have such an easy ride when making their claims. It's true that German law has now concluded that if the gambling contract that the player makes with the company turns out to be unlawful in the country where they live, the player can claim their losses back. But only if the player themselves "did not act illegally," as Dünchheim put it.
"You also have to say: Many of these players deliberately went to games in this gray zone because the winnings are potentially bigger," he said. "Because the companies don't pay taxes."

"Then the defense team of the gambling company will of course say: 'You took part in an illegal game yourself, so you were acting illegally.' And this question of interpretation is not simple," he added. "It's a very interesting intellectual question, but it's also existential for the gambling companies."
Tipico's gambling gray zone

The Tipico case is perhaps particularly interesting in the German context because, although the company is based in Malta, it was founded in 2004 by a group of German lawyers. The company is a big employer, with several thousand employees worldwide, and has been a sponsor of more than one top German football club. Tipico has also said that it has rigorous consumer protection measures in place to identify and prevent dangerous betting behavior.

But there was some legal ambiguity about its online operations in Germany up until 2021. "They always had lawyers who could attest that what they are doing conforms to European law, because it is permitted in a European Union member state," said Dünchheim. "But that is a false assumption, as it has now been established that a gambling permit in another EU state doesn't apply in Germany, because unlike other areas, gambling law isn't harmonized across the bloc."

"Tipico was started by two businessmen and grew big in a gray zone," as Dünchheim put it. "They had professional lobbying firms on board and they hired experienced lawyers, they had private equity firms on board. But of course they are carrying a huge financial risk."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: COA flags Sandiganbayan over P11.8M in foreign travel cash advances
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged the Sandiganbayan over P11.8 million in cash advances for officials" foreign trips in 2025 due to incomplete documentary requirements.

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 6:48pm
The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged the Sandiganbayan over P11.8 million in cash advances for officials’ foreign trips in 2025 due to incomplete documentary requirements.
In its annual audit report, COA said the cash advances covered seven foreign trips, including:

items: P2.84 million for attendance at the Court Technology Conference hosted by the National Center for State Courts in Kansas City, Missouri, United States, on September 16 to 18, 2025;
P365,767 for attendance at Hostile Environment Training in Victoria, Australia, on October 29 to November 2, 2025;
P2.57 million for four associate justices’ participation in a special course on the Basics of Artificial Intelligence for Criminal Legal Professionals in Budapest, Hungary, on October 13 to 14, 2025;

P3.18 million in cash advances for eight officials attending the International Association for Court Administration (IACA) conference on “Global Perspectives on Court Administration” in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, on November 15 to 20, 2025;

P440,076.17 for participation in another IACA conference in Dubai, titled “Global and Organizational Perspectives on Court Administration: Exploring Models, Maximizing Efficiency, and Embracing Technology,” on November 13 to 22, 2025;
P1.82 million for four associate justices’ attendance at the Judicial Executive Program 2025 hosted by the Singapore Judicial College on November 23 to 30, 2025; and
P636,148 for attendance at the 11th Session of the Conference of States Parties to the United Nations Convention against Corruption in Doha, Qatar, on December 14 to 22, 2025.

blocks.text: “The granting and liquidation of cash advances for official foreign travels of Sandiganbayan officials and employees for 2025, totaling over P11.8 million, were not fully supported with complete documentary requirements,” COA said.

The state auditors said this was contrary to Sections 1.1.4.2 and 1.2.4.2 of COA Circular No. 2012-001 dated June 14, 2012, "thereby limiting the verification of the validity and propriety of the transactions."
COA said the requests for cash advances lacked supporting documents, including formal letters of invitation, plane fare quotations, and flight itineraries.

While some transactions included program agendas or registration confirmations, COA said these did not replace the requirement for formal letters of invitation unless such letters could not be obtained.
The required airfare quotations and flight itineraries were also missing from the cash advance requests, restricting auditors’ ability to assess the reasonableness and economy of airfare expenses.

In response to COA’s inquiry, the Sandiganbayan accountant reportedly said airfare quotations were no longer required, adding that airlines were selected based on perceived safety considerations because “the safety of officials traveling abroad is prioritized in the booking of plane tickets.”
COA also found that liquidation reports covering P7.1 million of the P11.8 million in cash advances lacked the required narrative reports.
These reports are intended to document the activities undertaken and outcomes achieved during official trips.
Although certificates of appearance or attendance were attached, COA said these did not replace narrative reports, as both documents are required under COA Circular No. 2012-001.
“These documents are mandatory and complementary in nature, not alternative requirements,” COA said.
Sandiganbayan responds
In response to the audit findings, the Sandiganbayan said Thursday that the additional requirements sought by COA had been addressed.
The anti-graft court said it received a management letter dated September 8, 2026, on September 30, covering the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025.
“For CY 2025 transactions, we found no material misstatements in the Financial Statements that would warrant disclosure in this Management Letter (ML),” the Sandiganbayan quoted the letter as saying.
“The Sandiganbayan generally complied with the accounting policies and guidelines,” it added. —VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests
articles.summary:
Demonstrators are demanding resignation of Edi Rama after three days of clashes in Tirana

Albania’s prime minister, Edi Rama, has said he will not resign over student-led demonstrations, as…
articles.byline: Guardian staff and agencies in Tirana

blocks.text: Albania’s prime minister, Edi Rama, has said he will not resign over student-led demonstrations, as protesters and police clashed in the country’s capital for a third consecutive day.
Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse demonstrators marching along several main roads around Tirana, while protests spread to other cities.
Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation and more support for students in the country, citing poor university conditions and high tuition fees.
“As for calls for my resignation, governments are changed through democratic elections. ⁠We had elections last year, not a revolution,” Rama said in written ​responses to Reuters.

“My responsibility ‌is to listen, address ‌legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal ‌of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on European Union membership.”

Rama said he would be ready to discuss the rising cost of education, but added: “Attacking institutions, destroying public property and threatening public safety have nothing to do with the legitimate ‌demands of students.”

blocks.caption: Anti-government protest in Tirana. Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters

blocks.text: There were hours of violent clashes between police and demonstrators in Tirana on Tuesday and Wednesday, when protesters smashed their way into several government buildings and set at least one on fire.
Police said 51 officers were injured during Wednesday’s protests and 65 people were arrested on suspicion of “attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property”.
Police did not give figures for the number of protesters hurt but Tirana public hospital reported that “seven protesters injured in the violence sought medical treatment”.
The protests mark the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who won a fourth term last year.

The unrest ​follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a luxury resort on Albania’s southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, a project that has faced legal challenges.
“Corruption must be ⁠confronted and, as the EU itself has recently reaffirmed, Albania is ​tackling it as ​never before,” Rama said.
“Perhaps some ​forces, at home and abroad, do not want Albania to ​succeed as ‌a forerunner for ​EU membership. ​But I will not allow violence to derail Albania’s European future.”
The EU’s delegation in Tirana repeated its earlier calls for de-escalation, strongly condemning the “violent escalation at the protest and the destruction of public and private property”.
“We call on protesters to exercise restraint and to refrain from any acts of violence. Violence has no place in democracies,” it said in a statement.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the EU accession process among Balkan countries and is aiming for entry as early as 2028.

articles.title: Malacañang: Marcos listens to legit concerns about his governance
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. listens to the public's valid concerns about his governance, Malacañang said Thursday, following the release of Pulse Asia's latest trust and approval…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 6:31pm

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. listens to the public's valid concerns about his governance, Malacañang said Thursday, following the release of Pulse Asia's latest trust and approval ratings of the government's highest officials.

In a press brieifing, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said these concerns include the call for a fare hike and the need to lower electricity rates, both of which were not prompted by surveys.
"Patungkol sa mga ganyan, mayroon tayong nadidinig, mga lehitimong panawagan," Castro said.
(On matters like these, we hear legitimate calls from the public.)

Released on Thursday, a survey of Pulse Asia Research Inc. showed that trust and approval ratings of the President rose slightly, while Vice President Sara Duterte's counterpart numbers declined in September 2026.

The survey, conducted from September 17 to 24, 2026, found that Marcos' approval and trust ratings both climbed 1 percentage point to 30% and 29%, respectively. Compared to July 2026, the September 2026 survey showed that Marcos' disapproval rating slightly dipped by 3 percentage points.
However, nearly half of Filipino adults, or 48%, were found to distrust Marcos. Only 29% showed big trust in him, while 22% were undecided.
Balancing act
Castro explained that, like in implementing a fare hike, the President aims to balance the need to address the public's concerns with other considerations.
"Binabalanse ng Pangulo ang mga sinasagawang proyekto at programa. Hindi pwedeng isa lang 'yung nanalo, lahat dapat na nanalo. So ito 'yung mga bagay-bagay na the President listens," Castro said.
(The President balances the implementation of projects and programs. It cannot be that only one side benefits; everyone should benefit. These are the things that the President listens to.)
To recall, Marcos said his administration does not perform based on surveys.
"Hindi ganoon ang approach namin. We don't work according to surveys, not really," Marcos said.
"What we do is… 'Pag may nagrereklamo sinasabi, mahaba ang pila sa PhilHealth, ano ang puwede nating gawin para mas maginhawa?" the President said.

(That's not our approach. We don't work according to surveys, not really. What we do is... if there are complaints and they say there's a long line at PhilHealth, we study what can we do to ease this.)
Easing hunger
Following the Social Weather Stations' (SWS) survey on hunger, Castro said it is important to identify the areas most affected by hunger to determine where assistance should be targeted.

"Mas gugustuhin nating malaman sa result na ito saan 'yung lugar na apektado pa ng sinasabing kagutuman. Baka ito 'yung mga lugar na hindi pa naabot or nakapag-a-avail ng mga programa ng gobyerno," Castro said.
(We would rather use these results to identify areas still affected by hunger, as these may be places that have yet to be reached by or benefit from government programs.)

She also cited government programs in addressing hunger, including the Walang Gutom Program, Food Stamp Program, Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipnos Program, and Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers.
An SWS report showed that the number of Filipino families who experienced hunger rose in the past three months compared with the second quarter of 2026.
It showed that 22.6% of Filipino families experienced involuntary hunger at least once in the past three months, which is 2.3 percentage points up from 20.3% in June 2026. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine to restart strikes on Russian oil refineries, Zelensky says
articles.summary: Russia reports a Ukrainian strike on an oil refinery on Thursday, after Ukraine's president says a pause is over following fresh Russian attacks.

blocks.text: Ukraine will resume strikes on Russian oil refineries, Volodymyr Zelensky has said, as he accused the US of withdrawing crucial support.

The Ukrainian president said he had restricted such attacks for three days at Washington's behest, while Russia had continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times, external.

Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing on Russian strikes to pressure Kyiv into ending the attacks altogether after it struck a deal to import Russian diesel, and said restrictions to Starlink satellite services used by Ukraine's military were deliberate.
The Kremlin said Ukraine had "attempted a large-scale attack" on an oil refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris had caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
Zelensky meanwhile said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.

But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
The Ukrainian leader told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".

Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.

After the unexpected restriction to the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection on Tuesday, there were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame. But owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this, suggesting it was the Trump administration's doing. Trump denied halting intelligence-sharing.
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defence told the BBC early on Thursday that Starshield's "operation while on the move" had been restored, referring to the the military-focused version of Starlink.
They said officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances behind yesterday's restrictions".

Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.

But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict has sent the cost of petrol - and in particular diesel - skyrocketing, souring his standing with the American public.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.

Ukrainian officials have said they were not warned before a speed limit was imposed on the Starlink uplink, whose sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US Department of Defense (DoD) contract.
Musk wrote on Wednesday that the systems were owned and controlled by the US government and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [Trump]."
The Trump administration has not commented on the issue. The BBC has approached the White House and the DoD for comment.

articles.title: Donald Trump claims ‘Iran war will end very soon’ as midterm rallies heat up – US politics live
articles.summary: The US president said that the war will end ‘as soon as I want it to end’ as the midterms take place under a cloud of economic uncertainty

blocks.text: Donald Trump claims Iran war 'will end very soon'

US president Donald Trump claimed the Iran war ‘will end very soon,’ as voters consider their options ahead of midterm elections that are taking place amid economic uncertainty and ongoing global conflict.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday evening, Trump said: “The Iran war will end very soon. It’s going to end very soon, as soon as I want it to end, it’ll end.” He added that Iran would “never have a nuclear weapon” and that oil prices would “drop like a rock”.

The US president has in recent weeks attempted to shift focus towards Ukraine, and has suggested that its attack on Russian refineries are responsible for rising fuel prices. His renewed messaging on Iran suggests that the price of daily goods – and gas at the tank – are having an impact at the polls.

Voting groups that are key to winning votes in the midterms are increasingly disenchanted with the economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian. Three in four Americans are now concerned about the potential for a recession.
Elsewhere:

items: James Talarico, the Texas Democratic nominee for Senate, faced a grilling from undecided voters on a range of issues from Gaza to his faith at a town hall. Something he emphasized was his aspiration to put residents above party allegiance.

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he felt ‘betrayed’ by the US after Ukraine’s military access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite was restricted. The US president has denied that the administration has cut intelligence sharing but Musk suggested on X that the US government was behind the restrictions.
Trump’s new press secretary Katie Zacharia is facing scrutiny over her claims that she’s a lawyer. Zacharia has clarified some of the questions but the big one remains: has she ever passed the bar?

articles.title: School roof collapse in Pakistan's Peshawar kills dozens of students and one teacher
articles.summary: Local authorities said more than 50 other people were injured in the disaster. Roof collapses have become increasingly common in Pakistan.

image.caption: Emergency services were working to clear the rubble, looking for more survivorsImage: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province's Emergency Service/AFP

blocks.text: Officials in Peshawar, Pakistan, confirmed on Thursday that at least 28 pupils under the age of 13 died when an elementary school roof collapsed in the Afridi Abad area of the city.

One teacher has also died, they said. The deceased, along with more than 50 other injured people, were brought to Lady Reading Hospital as rescue workers rushed to clear the rubble and search for more survivors.
"We have taken out ​at ‌least 45 children," said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan, but added that more children were thought to still be under the rubble.
From her hospital bed, a teacher told reporters that the school had three floors and more than 1,200 pupils and staff.
The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear.
Roof collapses becoming more regular
Local media in Pakistan noted that such incidents are becoming increasingly routine across the country, due to poor building standards and maintenance.

In July, three young girls were killed near Umerkot when the outer wall of a government school gave way. That same month, one child died and five were injured in Lahore when the roof of an under-construction private school collapsed.
One month earlier, 14 children were killed in a similar manner at a private tutoring facility in Lahore, which came shortly after yet another such incident in Dera Ghazi Khan.

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine resume energy strikes despite Trump warnings
articles.summary: Moscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineries

blocks.text: The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.

Moscow accused Ukraine of launching its first strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to. Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming that it was the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.

Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after halting those attacks to show that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.

Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics ⁠facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Wreckage of a Russian jet-powered drone lay inside a crater that appeared at the site of a residential area after a strike in Kyiv. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters

blocks.text: Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to the sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.

“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said, referring to a growing quarrel with the Trump administration. “Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies. We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”

Trump suddenly declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, writing on TruthSocial: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

Despite Trump’s claims, however, Russia continued to launch heavy strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, using hypersonic and ballistic missiles to target key Ukrainian power plants, leaving cities including Kyiv without power and water for hours. Ukraine said it would not strike Russian oil refineries in the interim in order to show that it was ready for negotiations.
But the White House piled pressure on Zelenskyy to capitulate to Russia by threatening to cut programmes to deliver arms to Ukraine and to stop sharing US battlefield intelligence with Ukraine.

The US appeared to make good on some threats. Ukraine said it had not received advance warning of Russian missile strikes for several days from the United States this week. And on Wednesday, Ukrainian soldiers also complained that their access to Starshield programmes controlled by the US military had been restricted, scuppering drone missions on the frontlines.

The feud between Zelenskyy and Trump has spun out of control over the last week. Trump, who believes that his support for Ukraine should come with a degree of control over the country’s leadership, has said that Ukraine should “get a new president”.
Asked on Thursday by Piers Morgan whether he felt betrayed, Zelenskyy said yes. “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner,” he said.
Musk, the powerful head of SpaceX, which produces the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military, has emerged as a top critic of Zelenskyy in the United States.

On Thursday, Musk denied throttling the Starlink systems and said they were controlled by the US government. But in a post commenting on a Zelenskyy statement that Ukraine would continue to fight until Russia’s defeat, he wrote: “And so the slaughter continues … Time for Zelensky to go.”

October 15, 2026
Alcohol ban comes into force at all German train stations

blocks.caption: A few dozen stations, including Cologne's main station, imposed the ban much earlier as part of a test phase [FILE: July 23, 2026]Image: Marc John/Bonn.digital/picture alliance

blocks.text: Alcohol bans came into force at all German train stations when the clock struck midnight and Thursday began.
All the roughly 5,700 stations across Germany, including the train platforms themselves, are now booze-free zones.

Pubs, restaurants and other such hospitality businesses at train stations are exceptions to the rule, though, and can still serve alcohol. Consumption of alcohol will also remain legal on many trains, with long distance ones still serving beers and other tipples at their on-board bistros.
Rail operator Deutsche Bahn says the change aims to make train stations safer and cleaner, and more pleasant places to spend time waiting for a (who knows, perhaps delayed) train.
Various misdemeanors and incidents had prompted discussions on alcohol at stations over the years, but two this year in particular brought the issues into sharp focus.

A 26-year-old security staff member for Deutsche Bahn was beaten and kicked by a drunken passenger when trying to check their ticket. During the struggle the train door buckled and opened, and the Bahn employee fell from the train, suffering severe injuries. Earlier in the year, a train conductor was killed when attacked by a man without a valid ticket.
The new rules are part of DB's house rules, rather than being criminal law — meaning that at least in the first instance it is a matter for Bahn security staff to enforce rather than police.

"The alcohol consumption ban applies at stations every day, also on days with major events," Bahn spokeswoman Anja Bröder said when asked about often beer-fueled train usage days, like when football fans flock to Bundesliga games.

Around 40 stations piloted the project for some time prior to its implementation, including some of the largest like Cologne, Munich, Hamburg and Berlin. DB says it has had positive experiences with the early experiments, reporting more peaceful stations with less litter and travelers and employees saying they preferred the atmosphere.

A federal group dedicated to helping the homeless has criticized the measure, however, saying that for homeless people with addiction illnesses, train stations often served as "important, weatherproof and comparatively safe places" to shelter. A spokeswoman also told the Rheinische Post newspaper that if they were driven from sites like train stations, it would be harder for social workers to locate them.

articles.title: Lacson to Sara Duterte spox: Correct misleading claim on VP impeach trial costs
articles.summary: Lacson disputed Panelo’s claims, saying Panelo could have made an “honest mistake” on his remarks as it “clearly refers to the legislative functions of the Senate” and…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 15, 2026 | 6:07pm
Sen. Panfilo Lacson speaks during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Panfilo "Ping" Lacson urged the spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte to correct his earlier claim that the Senate impeachment court wasted P500 million on the impeachment trial after the prosecution dropped three charges.

In a statement released on Wednesday, October 14, Lacson rejected the claim of Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. that the Senate impeachment court “wasted” about P25 million a day during the 20 trial days when it tackled the first two Articles of Impeachment.

On October 13, the Senate impeachment court approved the prosecution’s manifestation to withdraw Articles I, III and IV, referring to the alleged misuse of confidential funds, bribery and grave threats, leaving only the alleged unexplained wealth charge.
Duterte’s counsel criticized the prosecution’s move and called it “unfair,” saying it could possibly lead to a mistrial.
Panelo, meanwhile, questioned the “lack of outrage,” particularly among the Senate majority, in a statement.

“Twenty trial days were spent on Articles I (misused of confidential funds) and IV (grave threats) - articles the prosecution has now withdrawn. That is approximately P25 million in Senate operating cost per day, or P500 million of taxpayers’ money, consumed on charges that will never be voted on,” Panelo said.

Lacson disputed Panelo’s claims, saying Panelo could have made an “honest mistake” in his remarks, as the figure “clearly refers to the legislative functions of the Senate” and not to the impeachment trial.
“I urge the VP’s spokesman to rectify an obviously misleading figure of P500 million, as I assume it was an honest mistake on his part,” Lacson said.
Palace: No wasted ‘resources’
Malacañang also pushed back on Panelo's claim, saying no public funds or resources were ‘wasted’ on the impeachment trial.
Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said at a press briefing on Thursday, October 15, that government officials and witnesses participated during trial days when the dropped charges were discussed.
Castro also pointed out that the defense team did not object to the prosecution’s withdrawal of charges, adding that both parties were able to participate in examining the witness.
“So lahat po ng concerned na parties ay nag-participate. So walang maaaring masabing nasayang kung meron namang naipakitang mga facts, data na maaaring makapagpaliwanag sa taong-bayan,” Castro said.
(So all concerned parties participated. So there are no resources wasted if there are facts and data that could be used to help the public better understand [the trial].)

articles.title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
articles.summary: Residents have been told to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.

blocks.text: Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported.
A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement.
Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts.
Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut Gül to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted.

Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue.
Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding.
"I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X.
He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time.
The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said.

A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks.
More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces.

In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave.

articles.title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
articles.summary: Lula's supporters hope the measure will boost his popularity ahead of a presidential run-off in 10 days.
articles.byline: Vanessa Buschschlüter, Mariana Schreiber, Vitor Tavares

blocks.text: Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary.
The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988.
Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election.

Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off.

The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.
Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it.
The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one.
Flávio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote.

Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it."
The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters.
Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment.
Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers.
"It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media.
Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices.
But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work.
The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage.
The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating.
Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.
The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores.
"My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil.
"I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home."

articles.title: US officials considering ad campaign to urge South African Afrikaners to emigrate
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Trump has falsely claimed Afrikaners are facing ‘white genocide’, but very few have applied to live in US

The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of…

blocks.text: The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a media campaign in South Africa to figure out why more white Afrikaners are not applying to become refugees to the US, as Donald Trump had hoped.

State department officials, according to an August proposal seen by the Guardian, outlined a roughly $335,000 research and advertising effort after applications to the refugee program “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025. The document, written by the US mission in South Africa with a department research unit for the embassy in Pretoria, admits officials know little about why.
“There’s currently little research about why Afrikaners are not applying to request referral into the US Refugee Admissions Program,” the proposal reads.

The focus on Afrikaners flows from a February 2025 executive order directing officials to put Afrikaner resettlement first while the broader refugee program stayed suspended. Administration officials had said Afrikaners face racial discrimination and “white genocide”. The South African government has rejected the genocide claims, and experts have widely dismissed the idea that Afrikaners face targeted violence or genocide.

Last year, the president restricted refugee admissions to 7,500, the lowest in US history, then raised it to 17,500 in May, with the added slots again going primarily to Afrikaners. The overall cap was 125,000 under Joe Biden.

The US admitted 16,292 refugees in the fiscal year that ended 30 September, according to its most recent data reporting. The remaining five were Afghans: three from last November and two from September. A year earlier, South Africans made up 342 of 38,102 refugee admissions.

The state department plan would proceed in three phases. The pitch suggests focus groups would be held in Pretoria and Krugersdorp in Gauteng, Bloemfontein and Kroonstad in Free State, Stellenbosch and Worcester in Western Cape and Kimberley and Orania in the Northern Cape, with the latter being an Afrikaner-only separatist community. Every location would host two age groups, 20 to 35 and 40 to 55, with participants grouped by urban or rural setting and household income. A survey of 1,000 Afrikaners, online and offline, would then test which messages work in which communities.

The final phase is a six-month digital campaign, mostly in Afrikaans with possibly some English, aimed at Afrikaners “interested in migrating”. Because the community is hard to reach through conventional social and press channels, the proposal says, the department would hire an agency with local knowledge and use “trusted messengers”.

In response, a spokesperson with the state department said “we continue to process and admit as refugees Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping the threat of government-sponsored race-based discrimination”.

“President Trump has been very clear that we are prioritizing the resettlement of Afrikaners in South Africa who are escaping government-sponsored race-based discrimination,” as part of US policy from the executive order, the spokesperson added.

Trump’s 2025 order alleged “South Africa has taken aggressive positions towards the United States and its allies, including accusing Israel, not Hamas, of genocide in the International Court of Justice, and reinvigorating its relations with Iran to develop commercial, military, and nuclear arrangements.”

This year’s Nobel peace prize went to Navi Pillay, the South African judge who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza, causing Trump to rave on Truth Social: “I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else!” and that the prize should have gone to “the Great United States of America, whose Representative, ME, settled eight Wars, and many other things”.

The South African government, for its part, has rejected the claim of genocide as unfounded and politically motivated. In New York last month, foreign minister Ronald Lamola said “there is no evidence” for the genocide claim. Pretoria has also argued that few South Africans have taken up the offer, which it says shows the claims are false.

The refugee program is one piece in a broader rupture. Trump announced last November that South Africa would not be invited to the 2026 G20 summit, which the US is hosting in Miami in mid-December, citing alleged abuses against white farmers. Washington has also cut aid and restricted visas over South Africa’s race and land policies.

Last month, the US ambassador in Pretoria, Leo Brent Bozell III, wrote in an op-ed that his government was “shocked” by what it saw as Pretoria’s silence on a set of US requests. He cited concern over the country’s 2024 Expropriation Act and a push to make rural crime a priority.

The administration is also putting money behind the cause. Just before funds expired, it moved to direct more than $175m from the state department’s Human Rights and Democracy Fund to 43 grants worth $176.9m, as the Guardian has reported. That is most of the $205m Congress appropriated for the fund, which bolsters rightwing causes abroad.

One is a $1m grant meant for “advancing white Afrikaner rights” in South Africa and for collecting data on abuses against minorities. No recipient has been named. Sources with knowledge of the awards process told the Guardian that administration figures lobbied personally for the awards, reflecting the priorities of JD Vance on European cultural identity and Stephen Miller on immigration and support for white minorities.
The bureau that runs refugee admissions has new leadership. Adam Zerbinopoulos, a career diplomat, became its senior official on 31 August.

articles.title: [READOUT] What a stickier inflation wave could mean for businesses
articles.summary: Businesses must brace for further risks from transport fares, electricity, wages, El Niño, and a weak peso

blocks.text: September’s 7.2% inflation rate was bad enough on its own. For businesses, the bigger concern is that price pressures could spread beyond the food and fuel shocks that first pushed inflation higher.

Seasonally adjusted inflation accelerated to 1.1% month on month in September from 0.5% in August. In what National Statistician Dennis Mapa described as a relatively “rare” broad increase, 11 of 13 major commodity groups posted faster inflation, while 16 of 18 regions saw inflation pick up. Core inflation also climbed to 4.7%, its highest in three years.

Nerve spoke with three economists to understand whether this is turning into a more persistent inflation problem and what businesses should prepare for heading into 2027. None sees a prolonged second wave as inevitable, but the risk is becoming harder to dismiss.
The September uptick comes as several price increases have yet to fully work their way through the economy. Among them:

items: Recent jeepney, bus, and taxi fare hikes were barely captured by the Philippine Statistics Authority in September and should show up more clearly in October. Passenger transport by road carries a 3.5% weight in the inflation basket.

Meralco has won approval to raise its average distribution rate from P1.35 to P1.48 per kilowatt-hour, its first increase after a rate review in 15 years. Once implemented in November, that increases energy costs for households and businesses.
The P60 minimum wage increase in Metro Manila took effect only on September 26, which means possible cost pass-through could be reflected in later months.

El Niño could add another supply shock into early 2027, with economists warning that a strong drought could cut rice and other food production across the Philippines and the region while also putting pressure on power supply and electricity costs.
The weakness of the Philippine peso is another source of inflation, as it raises the peso cost of imported fuel, food, raw materials, and equipment and could keep feeding into domestic prices.

blocks.text: Mapa pointed to energy, transport, and housing rents as some of the harder pressures to unwind. Electricity inflation was already 14.6% in September, while rents rose 4% and carry more than a 12% weight in the consumer price basket.
SM Investments Corporation group economist Robert Dan Roces expects inflation to remain a concern, but said much will depend on food and energy prices over the coming months.
“Some businesses may feel the pressure, but demand should remain relatively resilient,” he told Nerve.

RCBC chief economist Michael Ricafort told Nerve that inflation may pick up further in the coming months “in view of second-round inflation effects or higher prices of other affected goods and services, or pass-through effects, especially due to higher minimum wages.”

Meanwhile, Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan said a second, stickier wave becomes more plausible if higher food, fuel, electricity, and transport costs begin feeding into other prices and keep inflation expectations elevated.

Agriculture, transport, food businesses, and energy-intensive manufacturing face the most direct exposure, while smaller firms have less room to absorb higher costs. Manufacturing may be especially vulnerable given that the sector was already weakening before the latest inflation pressures intensified, with employment falling to 3.16 million in August from 3.43 million in July and 3.46 million in June.
“Small businesses, meanwhile, have less room to absorb higher costs, and retailers could suffer as households spend more on necessities and cut back elsewhere,” Punongbayan told Rappler.

Even as the “ber” months go by, retailers may need to temper expectations for the usual consumption boost. Consider that inflation among the bottom 30% of households reached 9% in September, compared with 7.2% nationally, leaving lower-income consumers with even less room for discretionary spending.
Forecasts vary considerably on how quickly inflation will ease in 2027, with Ricafort taking the most pessimistic view while institutional forecasts generally cluster between 4% and 5.4%.
High inflation also creates a second problem for businesses through interest rates. Here’s how economists think the BSP will react:

items: Roces expects the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) to be more cautious in putting too much additional pressure on growth.

Ricafort is more hawkish, seeing scope for further tightening while inflation remains far above the 2% to 4% target. He also noted that the BSP could partly match future US Federal Reserve hikes to manage interest rate differentials and help stabilize the peso.

Punongbayan said further hikes are possible and easing could be pushed into 2027 depending on how core inflation and expectations go, though higher key policy rates risk further straining borrowing, investment, and growth without fixing supply-side pressures.

blocks.text: The next BSP policy decision is scheduled for October 22, with another Monetary Board meeting set for December 17.
We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.

articles.title: Brazil's elections matter for the planet. This is why.
articles.summary: Brazil is heading back to the polls, but the impact could be felt worldwide. With the Amazon vital to the health of the planet, the election could help shape its future.

image.caption: Around 60% of the Amazon rainforest is within Brazil's bordersImage: Paralaxis/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are few national elections that carry as much environmental weight as Brazil's presidential race. And this one is being watched from far beyond the country's boundaries.
Home to the largest section of the Amazon rainforest, Brazil is guardian of a carbon sink of vital importance, making the country's conservation policies globally relevant.

Environmentalists have already voiced alarm at Flávio Bolsonaro — son of right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro — coming out 2% ahead of incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of elections.
"It's going to be a second coming of Bolsonaro, therefore a more radical Bolsonaro," said Claudio Angelo, international policy coordinator at Climate Observatory, a network of Brazilian NGOs.
"At the risk of sounding alarmist, I would say Lula's re-election is the only thing standing between us and the end of the Amazon."
One of nature's most powerful defenses
The Amazon rainforest stores huge amounts of the carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere from the burning of fossil fuels. As a result, it helps regulate the Earth's climate.

blocks.caption: Parts of the Amazon rainforest have been burned down to make way for cattle farms.Image: Andre Penner/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For decades, the tropical forest has acted as one of nature's most powerful defenses against climate change. But it has also suffered from widespread deforestation.
During Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, from 2019 until 2023, environmental agencies were weakened and enforcement efforts curtailed, meaning tropical forest was cleared at unprecedented rates.

"The environment agenda was disregarded and the level of control the government had on pollution overall, but specifically on deforestation, was reversed," said Claudio Forner, head of climate policy at Berlin-based think tank, Climate Analytics.

Over Bolsonaro's four-year term, an estimated 45,586km2 of the Amazon was destroyed, an area bigger than the size of Denmark. And the forest is not as resilient as it once was, with scientists warning that parts of it are now emitting more carbon than they absorb.

Lula came to office with a message of protection for the Amazon. Besides calling for an end to deforestation by 2030, he increased monitoring of the forest and strengthened Brazil's environmental enforcement agency IBAMA.
Deforestation has plummeted under his leadership, with 2026 set to be its lowest level in a decade. That represents a 41% drop overall compared to Jair Bolsonaro's tenure.
Pitting environment against the economy

Experts have already criticized Flávio Bolsonaro's record on forest protection. As a senator in 2019, he authored draft legislation that could have stark impacts for the Amazon. While landowners are currently required to preserve 80% of their property for the growth of native plants, the bill would allow them to use their holdings as they please.
"The signal from the president will say 'now you can deforest' or 'it's harder to deforest'," said Ana Yang, director of the Environment and Society Centre at London-based think tank Chatham House.
"The moment that you decrease enforcement capability, deforestation grows," she told DW.

blocks.caption: Thousands of students have marched in Rio de Janiero protesting against the possibility of Flávio Bolsonaro as president following the first round of electionsImage: Mariana Greif/JNA PRESS/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Bolsonaro has also pledged to end illegal deforestation by 2029, a year before Lula. But Claudio Angelo is critical of that message.
"He will end illegal deforestation not by enforcing the law, but by making it legal," he said.
More generally, environmental experts fear Bolsonaro might dismantle many of the protections strengthened under the current president.

"Unfortunately, climate change has become a partisan issue, so rather than offering a solution from their perspective, the right pictures climate change as an invented problem...that regulation goes against economic growth or it goes against competitiveness, that it's the aim of the left to control the means of production," Forner said.
In an interview with Brazilian media in August, Bolsonaro said he regarded extreme weather events to be cyclical and did not believe they were solely linked to human influence.
No straightforward climate success story

A Bolsonaro win is likely to see Brazil move away from its position as a climate leader, a role the country embraced last year as it hosted the COP30 climate conference in the Amazonian city of Belem.

But even a Lula victory would not represent a straightforward climate success story, say experts. While the current administration has overseen significant reductions in deforestation, it has also backed plans to expand oil production.

blocks.caption: Storing vast amounts of CO2, the Amazon rainforest is often referred to as the lung of the Earth Image: AP

blocks.text: Angelo said the decision to allow exploratory drilling was a "betrayal" of Lula's mandate but added that the president's overall record on climate had been "quite impressive".
"Lula is the world's worst climate leader, except for all the others," he told DW.

The current president will face a runoff election with Bolsonaro on October 25th. But while experts say the outcome could determine the fate of the Amazon and the wider efforts to curb global warming, for many Brazilians, climate is not high on their list of priorities.

"Ultimately what people care about is access to education, sanitation and health," said Yang. A road built through the Amazon, to access those services, while criticized from outside Brazil for destroying parts of the rainforest, would be desirable to voters, she added.
"They don't have time to care. Not because they don't want to. They care about their own survival," she said.
Report COP30 Brazil: Protect forests while drilling for oil?

articles.title: Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson to be sentenced for child sexual abuse – latest updates
articles.summary:
Donaldson has been found guilty of 18 counts of sexual abuse against two women when they were children and has been told he faces a lengthy jail term

A prison van believed to be carrying…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 12m agoDonaldson arrives at court in prison van
13m agoFormer DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson to be sentenced for child sexual abuse

blocks.text: Donaldson arrives at court in prison van
A prison van believed to be carrying Jeffrey Donaldson has arrived at Newry crown court.
He was being held at Maghaberry prison in his former parliamentary constituency of Lagan Valley in County Antrim awaiting sentencing.

blocks.caption: A prison van, believed to be carrying former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson, 63, arrives at Newry crown court ahead of his sentencing. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson to be sentenced for child sexual abuse
Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) in Northern Ireland, will be sentenced today for a string of sex offences against two women when they were children.

Donaldson, 63, will appear in Newry crown court after being found guilty earlier this year of 18 counts of sexual abuse including one count of rape against the women. The offences were committed between 1985 and 2008.

Extracts of the victim impact statements were read out in court by prosecution counsel Rosemary Walsh during a pre-sentencing hearing last month. One of the victims, Complainant B, described how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” and sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”. Complainant A wrote in her statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger.
Kieran Vaughan, mitigating for Donaldson, said during that hearing that the former Lagan Valley MP was a man of “previous good character” who “did achieve significant things”.

blocks.caption: Court artist drawing of former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson appearing at Newry crown court on 25 September 2026. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

blocks.text: But he added: “These convictions obliterate all those achievements he has made in his life.”
Judge Paul Ramsey previously told Donaldson that he would face a “lengthy sentence”.

Donaldson led the DUP from 2021 until 2024 when he was charged with historical sexual offences. He denied the charges but a jury convicted him in June of one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency.
Since his conviction, he has been stripped of his knighthood and removed from the privy council.

Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, 60, was found unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds. She faced a trial of the facts, which can test evidence but not result in a criminal conviction, and was found to have aided and abetted her husband’s offending.
She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge. The judge is due to decide on this at a later date.
She has lodged an appeal to have the court conclusions overturned.

articles.title: SC applicants weigh in on raising qualifications of nat'l candidates
articles.summary: The final batch of applicants vying for the Supreme Court (SC) position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier on Thursday weighed in on increasing the qualifications required…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 5:39pm

The final batch of applicants vying for the Supreme Court (SC) position that will be vacated by Associate Justice Amy Lazaro-Javier on Thursday weighed in on increasing the qualifications required for national elective positions in government.

For the second batch, Commission on Audit (COA) chairperson Gamaliel Cordoba, Government Corporate Counsel Solomon Hermosura, lawyer German Lichauco II, and Commission on Elections Commissioner Ernesto Maceda faced the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC).
Lichauco said that amending the Constitution was "long overdue."

"By putting up the bar, we will be able to weed out the possible candidates who are not qualified for such position. By raising the bar, upgrading the qualification, then we are now being given a greater position to choose wisely," he said.

"Fortunately, unfortunately… our electoral system is based on popularity and because of that, certain individuals who may not even be qualified for certain positions are elected simply because the masses see, the masses know of them, and the masses think that what they see is actually the person they are voting," he said.
Lichauco said that with more qualifications, the public has a better opportunity to choose wisely.

Under the 1987 Constitution, individuals seeking to be president, vice president, senator, and congressman must be a natural-born citizen and must be literate while each position has a varying requirement on age and residency in the country.
Cordoba also said he was in favor of increasing the qualifications.

"Because the complexity of governance is quite different right now. We're governing around 120 million people and the needs and the wants and the desires are different from maybe 10, 5, 20 years ago," he said.
"So the demands on the candidates, on the executive elected officials are quite high (so) I agree with that," he added.
However, Cordoba stressed that the qualifications cannot be amended simply through judicial legislation.
"It has to go through a constitutional charter change," he said.
Meanwhile, Maceda and Hermosura believe that there is no need to raise the qualifications.
"I am more comfortable with lesser qualification than with more," Maceda said.
"That's more democratic. It allows more participation and it does not impose limitations," he added.
According to Maceda, the right of people to vote and the right to run for public office should be given equal weight.

"The popular position nowadays are to require educational, to demand educational requirements. Unless it is shown that that's a guarantee of better service, then I don't see how that should supplant the existing order," he said.
Hermosura, meanwhile, said he was not in favor of too many qualifications, saying that in the private sector, the focus is on past performance and not on qualifications.
He also expressed hope that raising qualifications for national elective positions will not restrict access to public service.
He said that sometimes, meeting the qualifications requires a certain degree of financial stability.

The JBC panel was composed of Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Batangas Representative Gerville Luistro, former Supreme Court associate justice Jose Catral Mendoza, Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Erlinda Piñera Uy, lawyer Nesauro Hernandez Firme, and lawyer Jose Mejia.
Lazaro-Javier is set to restire on November 16, 2026. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian looks into 'wacky' photos taken in Senate session hall
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Thursday said he has asked the Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms (OSAA) to look into the circulating photos of certain individuals doing wacky poses while inside…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 5:25pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Thursday said he has asked the Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms (OSAA) to look into the circulating photos of certain individuals doing wacky poses while inside the session hall.
The Senate President did not drop any names, but wacky photos of the House prosecution panel recently circulated on social media.

“Ang session hall at Senado ay sagrado ito dahil dito natin ginagawa marami sa mga mahahalaga nating batas, mga pinaguusapan nating mahahalagang issues. So dapat respetuhin natin itong institusyon na ito. Hindi naman tama na may ginagawa kang katawa-tawa sa loob ng ating institusyon,” Gatchalian said in an ambush interview.

(The Senate and the session hall are sacred. It is where we craft many of our important laws and deliberate on significant issues. Therefore, we must respect this institution. It is simply not right to engage in ridiculous behavior while inside our institution.)

“So pinapa-check ko sa CCTV kung totoo ‘yun. Kasi ngayon uso ang AI eh, to be honest about it. I want to make sure lang na hindi AI ‘yun, hindi ‘yung ginawa sa lang sa photoshop. I'll reply to that,” he added.
(I’m having the CCTV footage checked to verify if it’s true. To be honest, AI is quite prevalent these days. I just want to ensure that it isn’t AI-generated or photoshopped. I will respond to that.)
Gatchalian said that the same applies to those who dance in the hallways of the Senate or those who sleep inside the session hall.
“Hindi pwedeng gumawa ng mga katawa-tawang mga aksyon sa Senado,” he emphasized.
(We can’t do ridiculous actions inside the Senate.)
“Hindi tama ‘yun. Pinapaimbestigahan ko na ngayon sa OSAA. Pinapatingin ko sa CCTV, just to make sure na hindi AI ‘yun o photoshopped,” he added.
(That’s not right. I’ve asked the OSAA to investigate and look at the CCTVs just to make sure those are not AI or photoshopped.)
If the photos and videos are proven authentic, the Senate President said he will issue a statement regarding the matter.
“Susulatan sila, bibigyan ng warning,” Gatchalian said.
(They will be issued a warning letter.) — RSJ, GMA News
