articles.title: Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
articles.summary: Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour, fire-and-brimstone documentary Musk — on tech oligarch, worlds-richest-man Elon Musk — is not uplifting. Instead, it is one of the most depressing and terrifying…

image.caption: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk walks to the stage to speak alongside Republican presidential nominee and former U.S. president Donald Trump at a campaign event at the Butler Farm Show in October 2024, in Butler, Pa. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour, fire-and-brimstone documentary Musk — about tech oligarch and the world's richest man Elon Musk — is not uplifting. Instead, it is one of the most depressing and terrifying pieces of public media since An Inconvenient Truth alerted a largely unaware public to its imminent annihilation by climate change.

Unlike An Inconvenient Truth, Gibney's Musk does not appear to offer a hopeful final message about how we might get out of this mess. Instead, we get an outline of how, in Gibney's view, Musk rose from upstart entrepreneur to political arriviste who orchestrated the dismantling of USAID, then attempted to create a baby farm and commune to survive a supposed civil war. That is all before, we are to believe, he supposedly upended all of Western democracy.

Sitting for an interview this September ahead of the film's showing at the Toronto International Film Festival, Gibney was not too surprised by the dour perception: he had spent the previous few days fielding defamation lawsuit threats from a similarly unhappy Musk, after all. That is along with Musk's descriptions of Gibney as "a shill for the far left," "horrible human" and, simply, a "douche."

Gibney also acknowledged the foreboding length: it was only after they finished their original two-hour feature that Musk allied himself with U.S. President Donald Trump. At that point, he said, HBO executives told Gibney they needed to expand the work, using it as a "building block for a much more epic drama … For this figure, who has so much influence on the future of the planet, it's deserving of that three hours and 45 minutes."

That relationship proved fraught on its own. The film hits North American theatres Oct. 16, but — at the time of the interview — Gibney was nervous. The international rights-holder, Universal, hadn't confirmed whether it would even distribute the film outside North America, given the potential of political pressure.

At the same time, he said Paramount's acquisition of HBO parent company Warner — with Paramount controlled by the Trump-friendly David Ellison — had him "concerned in the back of [his] mind" that the documentary's streaming release could be scuppered entirely.

Since that interview, Gibney has said international theatrical release plans are now being discussed; the documentary is slated for an early 2027 streaming release, though no specific date has been given. When, or if, audiences do see it, he hopes the reception isn't quite so bleak.

"It's not a funeral; it's a warning. But things are pretty dark. We're going to be lowered into the earth if we're not careful," the director said, even while recognizing the sheer inescapability of dread his film tends to elicit. "You know, and the film ends with the planet Earth exploding and Musk escaping on his spaceship. So that's about as pessimistic as it gets."
A question of objectivity

Though he started the project as an avowed Musk fan — a Tesla solar panel system-owner and all — by the time he began working on it in earnest, he says, any benefit of the doubt he had extended to his subject had evaporated. When he reached out to interview Musk himself, he said he was stonewalled.

Director Alex Gibney poses for portrait photographs for the film Musk during the 83rd edition of the Venice Film Festival in Venice, Italy, in September 2026. (Scott A Garfitt/Invision/The Associated Press)
Outreach to those around Musk was similarly stymied: close business associates uniformly refused to speak without his permission. The workaround was to instead give Musk a voice of his own.

An AI-avatar, using Musk's own statements, narrates much of the documentary. Much of what it says, like the real Musk's statements about the "hit piece" Gibney came out with, is overtly critical of the documentary's framing.
The result is a somewhat bifurcated, but overwhelmingly negative picture of a man Gibney asserts is at the centre of modern politics' downfall.

There is the charting of Musk's early history as a self-described "founder" at Paypal and Tesla — including interviews ranging from journalists covering him at the time to his former wife, Justine Musk — that characterize his public persona as an engineer and genius as little more than a PR-crafted lie.

"There is a kind of generalised notion in modern societies that if you're rich, you must be very smart — you must be a genius," Gibney says, sharing the central thesis of the documentary. "But maybe you're just ruthless. And maybe you can be very rich and very powerful — and also, to some extent, unhinged."
And then there is Musk's time at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and, in Gibney's telling, his role as an architect of the dismantling of the U.S. federal government.

items: TikTok, X reportedly barring ads for documentary about Elon Musk
Elon Musk calls documentary about him a 'hit piece' after buzzy debut

blocks.text: The film includes accusations from former MAGA influencer Ashley St. Clair, the mother to one of Musk's children, who speaks about cryptic text messages Musk sent her ahead of the 2024 U.S. presidential election that saw Trump re-elected — messages that include references to an "anomaly in the Matrix" created by "ten thousand lasers in space."
Gibney then asks her whether she thinks that was a reference to SpaceX satellites. She responds: "I don't know where else he has lasers."
"I should point out that the remarks about the 'anomaly in the Matrix' and lasers from space didn't come from a critic of Musk. It didn't come from me; they came from Elon Musk himself," Gibney said.

That is despite a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions, claiming the exchange reinforces a disproven conspiracy theory that Musk used his internet provider, Starlink, to interfere with voting machines in swing states.
"That seems a legitimate thing to put in a film," Gibney said. "I don't say in the film that's what he did. I say that's been said."
Elon Musk steps down as top adviser to Trump

Similarly when pressed, Gibney defended the decision of including an AI-generated avatar in a documentary critical of an AI proponent: "We used some AI tools, but they're being used by — they're guided by human hands," he said. He explained that the idea was for it to serve as a sort of "agent provocateur" that foments a negative reaction to AI proliferation by forcing audiences to witness it.
When asked whether he hopes or theorizes that the film could affect people's votes ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterms, he has a simple response: "I do."

Because to Gibney, Musk's accumulation of power isn't just a failure on Musk's part. When "a reckless tech billionaire takes effective control of the federal government, and attempts to destroy it for personal aggrandisement," he says, Americans themselves bear responsibility.
"We did. We let him take it, because we didn't demand that our representatives hold him to account," he said.
"You know, 'Oh, I like my Tesla, so he must be a good guy.' Well, you may like your Tesla, but what if he's not a good guy, right?"

articles.title: In Unreliable Boyfriend, Chrystia Freeland details the rift between her and Trudeau
articles.summary: In Unreliable Boyfriend, one-time finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland digs into how her political relationship with Justin Trudeau went from a warm face-to-face invite into…

image.caption: Shown here in happier times in June 2017, Foreign Affairs Minister Chrystia Freeland and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau share a moment of unity in the House of Commons. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: In Unreliable Boyfriend, one-time finance minister and deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland digs into how her political relationship with Justin Trudeau went from a warm face-to-face invite into public service to a cold Zoom call where he booted her from the finance role years later.
While the book's "unreliable boyfriend" is the United States under U.S. President Donald Trump, readers could be forgiven for thinking the title is actually inspired by Trudeau.

She enthuses about how the pair worked together on the trade file, their management of the pandemic and their rollout of national child care. Yet she also details Trudeau's slide into unpopularity, penchant for humiliating members of his cabinet, word-policing and tendency to pick on those weaker than him.

While their relationship ended bitterly, she is still able to praise Trudeau for his strengths, one of which she noticed at a party in Toronto in late 2012, before Trudeau the Liberal MP became Trudeau the prime minister.
At that party celebrating the launch of Freeland's book Plutocrats, her father cornered Trudeau to convey his thoughts on politics, eager to speak with "Liberal political royalty."
"I was mortified," Freeland recalled as she rushed over to try and free Trudeau from her father's grip — only to learn that the future prime minister was enjoying the chat.
Justin Trudeau and Chrystia Freeland over the years
The following summer Freeland was invited to a breakfast that included Trudeau and former Ontario premier and current MP Bob Rae.
She was told Rae was stepping down from his Toronto seat and was asked if she'd consider running in an upcoming byelection.
"I spent the next six weeks agonizing over Justin's offer," she wrote.
She worried about uprooting her children from the life she and her husband had built for them in New York. And with the Liberals in third place, she knew she may be "joining a lost cause."
In the end she wrote that she was won over by "Trudeau's kindness to my dad" and her father's encouragement to accept the offer.
Knowing when to play hardball

One of Trump's first moves as president was to sign an executive order withdrawing the U.S. from the Trans Pacific Partnership (TPP) trade deal. By the spring of 2017, Trump was also threatening to pull out of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

The remaining TPP countries were set to sign the pact on the margins of a November summit in Da Nang, Vietnam. But Freeland, who was foreign affairs minister at the time, wrote that Trudeau wanted a better deal.
In a call with then international trade minister François-Philippe Champagne, Freeland and others, Trudeau humiliated Champagne for not securing concessions on intellectual property and other issues.

items: TPP faces uncertain future after Trudeau skips meeting
Partners reach agreement on 'core elements' of trade deal, Canada says

blocks.text: "I still cringe as I remember it — the embarrassment I felt at hearing a colleague humiliated reminded me of feeling bad for my childhood friends in Peace River when they got spanked while I was over to play."

When Canada refused to sign the deal, Freeland wrote Trudeau angered both Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe and Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull. Despite that pushback, Freeland said she admired the defiance.
"Trudeau showed that, love him or loathe him, you could not deny that he was a leader with balls," she wrote.
Freeland said with NAFTA talks coming up, it was important to let the White House know when it came to trade deals, Canada "was prepared to play hardball."
The 'FAFO' fight for free trade
By early 2018, Freeland wrote she had grown so "worried that American proposals could kill NAFTA" she'd begun writing a speech to deliver after its demise.

During particularly fraught meetings with U.S. officials in Washington, Freeland admitted she would occasionally "take refuge in the ladies' washroom" which was a safe place because, she said, there were almost never any women on the U.S. side of the table.
"Once, at a particularly dire moment, I got down on my knees on the cold white tiles in front of the sinks and prayed," she wrote.
Freeland said that Canada only managed to save that deal because it imposed retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. when it hit Canada with steel and aluminum tariffs, targeting key Republican districts.
That "FAFO" approach, and Trudeau's willingness to employ it, she wrote, was what ensured Canada got back to a "reciprocal relationship with our neighbour."

items: The evolution of Freeland's relationship with her U.S. counterpart
Freeland says renegotiated NAFTA was always going to come down to the wire

blocks.text: She said the details of the new NAFTA, an agreement Canadians now call the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), were largely left to her.
Trudeau "got extremely involved in the fine print of his own public appearances … on trade he didn't dive into the details," she said.
Still, she described the saving of NAFTA as "Trudeau's finest hour … the moment when Canada's playboy prince became a true national leader."
But Freeland says Trudeau's political stock was already in decline on another front thanks to his ill-fated trip to India.
Trudeau, his then wife Sophie Grégoire Trudeau and children Xavier and Ella-Grace are seen during their February 2018 trip to India. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

She described Trudeau's state visit to India in February 2018 as "a political disaster" where his over-the-top outfits became a distraction — and a Canadian of Indian descent, Jaspal Atwal, who was convicted of attempted murder for trying to assassinate an Indian cabinet minister, turned up at an official event.
Crying at cabinet meetings

Over the next few years, Trudeau landed achievements that Freeland wrote will be judged kindly by history. She praised him for his role in securing trade deals with the U.S., EU and the Pacific Rim countries, rolling out a national daycare program and managing the pandemic. But she noted that Canadians had started to sour on him for his "self-righteous exhibitionism."
"Crying was routine at cabinet meetings," she wrote. "There were always boxes of Kleenex on hand, and really sad colleagues would sometimes get a hug from the PM."
Freeland noted one moment when Trudeau gave a female colleague a "long, harsh public scolding" for describing something as crazy.
Trudeau apparently told the colleague that the term was a "derogatory adjective" that was "insulting to people with mental health issues."
The term Trudeau wanted them to use instead was "bananas."
Freeland receives applause from Trudeau after delivering her last federal budget in the House of Commons in 2024. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Freeland said she objected to "linguistic purity tests" because some people struggle to keep up — but her larger objection was about something else.
"I think what troubled me the most about the crying in cabinet and the lectures about word choice was that it sometimes went along with what seemed like bullying," she wrote.
While Freeland said she has no problem with trying to bully people like Trump or Vladimir Putin, she didn't like it when she saw Trudeau "pushing weaker people around."
Chrétien's advice

As the years rolled on and Trudeau's popularity declined, Freeland said she came to understand that Trudeau's gift of making strangers feel like "they are the most important person in the world" stopped short of his peers.

"We might walk together for the cameras but none of us, even his personal friends from childhood, had intimate political relationships with him," she wrote. "Few of us ever spent time with him one-on-one."

As rumours began to swirl that Trudeau was going to replace Freeland as finance minister with former central bank governor (and now prime minister) Mark Carney, she sought advice from former Liberal prime minister Jean Chrétien in November 2024.
She said Chrétien told her that her loyalty had reached its logical limit.

Freeland said Chrétien told her that as long as she remains in cabinet, and keeps publicly declaring she supports Trudeau, he would stay on as prime minister and the party would lose the next election.

"Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre will become prime minister and the Liberal Party will be devastated. And if that happens, it will be partly your fault, because your continued support is what is making it possible for Justin Trudeau to stay in office," she said Chrétien told her.
Prime Minister Mark Carney walks with Freeland after a cabinet meeting in September 2025. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Freeland was due to deliver her government's fall economic statement on Dec. 16. She wrote that with Trump set to be sworn in as president for the second time just weeks later, it was time to tighten up finances and prepare for what could be a protracted economic war.
Days before that statement was to be delivered, she said that Trudeau "removed over $12 billion in spending cuts" that Freeland had included to help prepare.
"I knew that, in this consequential moment, Trudeau was focused solely on his own political survival," she said. "And, in his desperation, he was doing increasingly stupid things."
The third-worst day of her life

On Friday the 13th — three days before she was set to deliver that economic statement — Trudeau arranged a Zoom call where she says he told her: "I no longer want you to serve as my finance minister."
She described it as the third-worst day of her life after the death of her mother and her parent's divorce.
Freeland says she was told she would retain the deputy prime minister title and would still be responsible for the Canada-U.S. relationship — but without a department to back her up.
When Freeland asked who would replace her, Trudeau told her it would be Carney.
Freeland wrote that Trudeau still wanted Freeland to deliver the economic statement and gave her time to think it over.
"Rather than be fired, I resigned," she wrote. "The Zoom call with Trudeau had taught me that I simply couldn't trust the PM — and that he had decided not to trust me."

items: Freeland's resignation pushes deficit news to the side
Government still planning to unveil economic statement
Chrystia Freeland to step down as MP on Friday

blocks.text: Describing her resignation from cabinet as "maybe the most significant resignation letter in Canadian political history," Freeland claimed credit for bringing down one prime minister, thwarting Poilievre's chance to become the next one and clearing the way for Carney to swoop in for the kill.
After the news hit, Freeland wrote that Chrétien called her and congratulated her for "doing the right thing."
Despite losing the subsequent Liberal leadership race to Carney, Freeland said she thinks she "could have won the 2025 election" and "been an effective PM."
Still, she said Carney is an "excellent" prime minister.
"I am proud my decision helped him get the top job, even though I ended up paying a pretty steep political price," she said.

articles.title: The 'leap second' could disappear. How a minor time adjustment became a major problem
articles.summary: For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth. On Thursday, an international time-keeping body in France is expected to do away…

image.caption: Clockmaker Scott Gow adjusts the hands of a clock at the Electric Time Company in Medfield, Mass., in 2024. An international body is voting Thursday to determine the future of 'leap second' time changes. (Charles Krupa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World

For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth. On Thursday, an international time-keeping body in France is expected to do away with leap seconds and let the clocks slip until they're out of alignment by a full hour — meaning it could be centuries, or even millennia, before another tweak is needed.
International time-keeping body may vote to ditch the decades-long tradition Thursday
For more than 50 years, humanity has used "leap seconds" to keep our clocks aligned with the rotation of the Earth.

On Thursday, an international timekeeping body in France is expected to do away with leap seconds and let the clocks slip until they're out of alignment by a full hour, which could take centuries or even millennia.

The precise atomic time we use to track our days — developed in the 1950s and measured by tracking the natural vibrations of atoms — is slightly out of sync with solar time, which is based on the position of the sun in the sky relative to a specific location on Earth, because the planet's rotation has been gradually slowing.

The leap second was introduced in 1972 as a way to correct the discrepancy. Ten seconds were added immediately, says Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre.

Since then, the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, which tracks the difference between the solar day and atomic time, has monitored the discrepancy to determine when an extra second is needed.

When that threshold is reached, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures adds a second at either the end of December or the end of June. Leap seconds have been added 27 times, most recently in 2016.

Scott Beattie, lead of the frequency and time team at the National Research Council of Canada's Metrology Research Centre, says leap seconds are becoming increasingly difficult to manage as more systems rely on precise timekeeping. (National Research Council Canada)

If we didn't make those tiny adjustments, nothing would perceptibly change in our lifetimes. But eventually, Beattie says, "you might get the brightest part of the day at midnight and the darkest part of day at noon."

The concept is similar to leap years, whereby a day is added to the end of February every four years to keep the Gregorian calendar aligned with the seasons because the Earth's orbit around the sun takes about 365¼ days.
Without leap years, our hottest months would eventually fall during what is now winter, and the colder months during summer, Beattie says.

items: Celebrating New Year's? You'll have to wait an extra second
2016 is getting a leap second

blocks.text: What's the problem?
But the time has come when leap seconds seem to be causing more trouble than they're worth.
"The basic global agreement is that we want to do away with these abrupt leap seconds," Beattie said.
That's because the small adjustment can be a headache for tech and telecommunications companies and infrastructure that relies on precise timekeeping.
Sleep experts say permanent daylight time could negatively impact kids
Companies also have different ways of implementing leap seconds, such as changing their clock rates to stretch the extra second over several hours or an entire day.
Beattie says that variation among networks creates a risk of system failures.
The leap second was blamed for Reddit and LinkedIn crashes in 2012, for example, and brief outages at Cloudflare in 2016.

"The problem is that the needs for timing and network synchronicity are just going up and up, they're ever increasing," Beattie said. "And so the risks are just increasing along with them, because all you need is for some system to not implement it properly and then you could have a cascade effect that could cause quite significant problems."
Negative seconds?
There's another complicating twist.

Over the last six years or so, the Earth's rotation has actually sped up, raising the possibility that a "negative leap second" — in which a second would be taken away — could be needed in the future.

Tech giant Meta said in 2022 that a negative leap second could have a "devastating effect" on software, adding, "In any case, every leap second is a major source of pain for people who manage hardware infrastructures."

items: Parts of northwestern Ontario moving to permanent daylight saving time in November
Seasonal time changes in N.W.T. officially end as of Nov. 1

blocks.text: The proposed fix, which would take effect in May 2027, is instead to let those extra seconds add up to 3,600 — a full hour — before adjusting the clocks, pushing the issue many generations down the road.
Not everyone is impressed by this approach.
Paul Delaney, a York University physics and astronomy professor emeritus, says he was "surprised" to hear the proposal.

"It is a problem for an increasingly computerized, AI-oriented economy, and that's obviously what we have," he said. "But that said, gosh, don't we still hire computer programmers to sort these sorts of things out? Some part of me says that we're throwing in the towel and saying, 'Oh, it's too difficult to do, and what the heck, it is just a second.'"
'Not a perfect system'

Samantha Lawler, an associate professor of astronomy at the University of Regina, says many factors affect the Earth's rotation speed, but it has tended to slow over time, in part because of the moon's effect on Earth's tides.
But complex variables, including climate change and glacial melting, can cause changes in that trend.

items: This is how fast Swiss glaciers, the 'water tower of Europe,' are melting away
Climate change past the point of no return, UN says, as worst impacts are now unavoidable

blocks.text: She says there is no perfect system for our clocks to account for these shifts and "we'll be fine" without leap seconds.

"This is a real human problem that we've been struggling with forever, as long as we've been watching the stars move across the sky and tracking when the sun rises and sets, and trying to get the patterns right," Lawler said.
"It's always going to be a little bit wrong, and I think we just have to accept that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Live Nation to relocate Backstreet Boys fans who say they got 'screwed' on seats with obstructed views
articles.summary: Dozens of fans flooded social media with complaints that Ticketmaster failed to label Backstreet Boys presale tickets appropriately, leaving some fans with seats with obstructed views. Live Nation…

blocks.text: Toronto

Dozens of fans flooded social media with complaints that Ticketmaster failed to label Backstreet Boys presale tickets appropriately, leaving some fans with seats with obstructed views. Live Nation now says fans whose seats are impacted "will be proactively relocated to comparable full-view locations."
Fans voiced concerns on social media after presale tickets sold without being labelled as obstructed
What these Toronto Backstreet Boys fans weren't told when they bought their concert tickets
When Tannia Ribeiro got through the Rogers presale queue for a chance to score tickets to see the Backstreet Boys in Toronto, she was ecstatic.

Many of the tickets were bought up by that point, but then she saw them: two tickets still available in the 130 section at Rogers Centre — perfect for her and her friend to catch the show together like they planned.
A near-$700 transaction later, Ribeiro, who's been a Backstreet Boys fan since the band's first album was released in 1996, was going to the show.
It wasn't until later that an Instagram post popped up on her feed, flagging that some seat areas, including hers, had an obstructed view of the stage.

Days after the presale ended, dozens of fans flooded social media with complaints that Ticketmaster failed to indicate their seats had an obstructed view and that after the presale, those seats were selling for a discounted price. That prompted calls for the vendor to issue an apology and rectify the problem, either through refunds or exchanges for different seats.
"As soon as I got it in writing [from Ticketmaster] that these seats are partially obstructed, that's when my heart dropped," Ribeiro said.
Ribeiro showed CBC News a screenshot of an email exchange this week with Ticketmaster confirming her seats were impacted.
In an emailed statement Wednesday, Live Nation acknowledged that "some" fans had raised concerns about their tickets.

"Fans whose seats are impacted will be proactively relocated to comparable full-view locations in advance of their show. We expect to begin reaching out to affected fans in the coming days with additional information," the company said.
The Backstreet Boys are expected to play 12 shows across four consecutive weekends in Toronto, from February to March 2027. (backstreetboys.com)
Rogers announced earlier this month that it was the organizer bringing the Backstreet Boys to Toronto in 2027. Its announcement offered Rogers customers "exclusive" access to the Oct. 5 presale.
Live Nation is the entertainment company overseeing the concerts, and its subsidiary, Ticketmaster, operates the ticketing platform for them.

Stephanie Tan, also a fan of the pop band, planned to fly in from Vancouver to catch the band's opening weekend show in Toronto. Later, she found out the seats she purchased had the same problem as Ribeiro's.
Given what she spent on four tickets, just over $3,000 after taxes and fees, Tan thought she'd be getting a "pretty amazing view."
But she said she later found out about the potential obstructed view for her seats from "online chatter" and said she only got that confirmation from Ticketmaster after she emailed them about it.
"I was honestly low-key pissed," she said.

Stephanie Tan says she was frustrated to find out that Backstreet Boys concert tickets she bought from a presale have now been identified as tickets that have an obstructed view. (Submitted by Stephanie Tan)
Screenshots show price discrepancy
Lisa Parent, a Backstreet Boys fan from Thunder Bay, Ont., bought eight tickets to the Feb. 20 show and is also feeling the frustration.

She said she only found out her seats had an obstructed view after she started looking into buying tickets for another show in March, and noticed the row she purchased tickets in was now labelled differently.
Parent provided screenshots to CBC News that showed the discrepancy.
A screenshot from the Oct. 5 presale shows Parent paid just over $5,500 for eight concert tickets for the Feb. 20 show, including fees and taxes.

A screenshot of emails from the same day shows Parent asking Ticketmaster for confirmation that her tickets have an unobstructed view. On Oct. 7, a Ticketmaster agent confirmed that her seats are "not located under obstructed view."

items: Backstreet Boys add multiple dates to planned Toronto concerts

blocks.text: But in a screenshot of the Ticketmaster website for a show on March 5, the same seats Parent bought for the Feb. 20 show had a "partially obstructed view" warning.
Those tickets were discounted, with eight totaling just over $2,900, about half of what Parent paid in the Feb. 20 show presale.
"I feel that I have been misled on what they have sold me on presale day," she said, adding she felt "tricked."
Ticketmaster, Rogers respond
In an emailed statement Wednesday, Ticketmaster said the Backstreet Boys tour is "working on a solution for the small number of fans affected by newly identified obstructed views."
"We thank fans for their patience," the statement said.
Charmaine Khan, spokesperson for Rogers, referred all questions to Live Nation and Ticketmaster.

items: Live Nation, Ticketmaster vow to fight breakup after monopoly verdict

blocks.text: Before Live Nation responded to CBC News, Tan said she would be disputing the cost of the tickets through her credit card company, while Parent said she would like a partial refund.
"What's fair is I picked those seats, and I would like to pay what they're worth today, which is half the price," Parent said.
Ribeiro said she wants Ticketmaster to issue the affected customers an apology.
"They really screwed us over," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

articles.title: DepEd welcomes first group of counselors hired after string of campus shootings
articles.summary: The Department of Education swore in some 300 newly hired school counselor associates and guidance counselors in Metro Manila on Thursday, October 15.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 3:53pm
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education swore in some 300 newly hired school counselor associates and guidance counselors in Metro Manila on Thursday, October 15.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara led the oath-taking of 339 school counselor associates at the DepEd central office in Pasig City. All are assigned to the National Capital Region.
The department has been in a time crunch to fill 10,000 new school counselor associate posts following a string of deadly campus shootings since June, all of which took place outside Metro Manila.

Before this, school shootings were considered rare in the Philippines, even as gun violence is not. Two of the three recent shooting incidents in schools were a result of minors gaining access to service-issued firearms.

The presence of mental health workers in schools is a "gap in our department," Angara told reporters in Filipino, crediting Undersecretary Wilfred Cabral, who heads the agency's human resources, for speeding up school counselor associates' recruitment.
"The president's order was: as soon as we can hire, we hire," Angara said. "This is just NCR, and it's already more than 300. We have a few thousand more on the way."
Cabral said 5,404 of the 10,000 school counselor associate posts had been filled, 4,423 were under assessment and 312 remained open for applications across the regions.

The new hires are now officially DepEd employees and are expected to report to schools "as soon as possible," Angara said. They hold plantilla, or permanent, positions at Salary Grade 11, with a basic monthly pay of about P31,000.
Angara said the associates would serve as "advisers" to students, watching for those who appear depressed, lost or disconnected from their school community, and stepping in to help.
Their role extends beyond career guidance to students' personal struggles and "all aspects" of their lives, the DepEd secretary said.
The associate post is new to DepEd, a position created under Republic Act 12080 or the Basic Education Mental Health and Well-being Promotion Act.
The law, signed in 2024, seeks to plug the long-standing shortage of registered guidance counselors in schools.

Difficulties hiring licensed counselors have been attributed to several factors, including the requirement that they hold a master's degree and the limited options for career progression. Based on a study by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2), the country produces only about 300 registered guidance counseling graduates a year.
As a result, fewer than 1,000 registered guidance counselors serve in DepEd, which runs more than 45,000 schools.
Meanwhile, associates need only a bachelor's degree in guidance and counseling or psychology, or a related degree with at least 18 units in those fields, plus 200 hours of supervised practicum.
Calls for DepEd to provide more mental health services in schools gained fresh urgency after three school shootings this year.
In June, three students were killed in a shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, and both suspects, students of the school, were arrested.
In August, a shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University's junior high school left two dead, including the gunman.
On September 18, a minor opened fire at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, leaving at least three dead, among them the shooter.
A Senate inquiry has linked the Tacloban attack to "764", an international online network accused of radicalizing children
Of the 5,000 guidance counselor posts created in 2020, only about 1,000 were filled, Cabral said in August.

The Department of Budget and Management authorized the creation of 10,000 school counselor associate positions on July 15. DepEd later cut the hiring process from three to four months to about 30 days.
The department has committed to lawmakers to fill the positions by December.
Even then, DepEd will fall far short of its needs, as Angara has confirmed the department needs a whopping 48,000 associates, one for every school, but its 2026 budget funds only 10,000.

articles.title: NBI chief Matibag says land titles of alleged Sara properties declared in SALN
articles.summary: National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag stood by the agency"s findings regarding properties being linked to Vice President Sara Duterte, calling her denial the “weakest form of…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 3:49pm

National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag stood by the agency’s findings regarding properties being linked to Vice President Sara Duterte, calling her denial the “weakest form of argument.”
In a news conference, Matibag referred to the Vice President's statement of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALN) that supposedly contained the details of the properties' land titles.

GMA News Online is seeking comment from the office of Sara Duterte, but the Vice President on Tuesday denied owning the properties associated to her by the NBI, calling the move a kind of “public deception.”

“Yun po yung claim ng Vice President. Hindi kanila yung property, hindi ba? Ang tanong ko ngayon, bakit niyo po idineklara sa SALN? Bakit po nandirito sa SALN? At naka-describe po sa SALN yung TCT (transfer of certification of title)?" Matibag said in a news conference.
"So ang ginawa po namin, kumuha kami ng copy ng TCT sa, sa LRA (Land Registration Authority). At pinuntahan namin yung lugar base do sa description sa TCT," he added.

(The Vice President claims that the property is not theirs. How come it was declared in the SALN and the TCT is described in the SALN? What we did was get a copy of the TCT from the LRA, and we went to the location of the property based on the description in the TCT).
Matibag said that the NBI has also geotagged the area and interviewed several residents in the area.
“Siguro kung wala kang depensa, pinaka reason mo is general denial, which is the weakest form of argument under the rules of evidence,” Matibag said,
(Maybe if you have no defense, your leading reason is general denial, which is the weakest form of argument under the rules of evidence.)
The NBI is investigating allegations of "land banking" on the part of some members of the Duterte family, based on the affidavit of dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.
Gracioso also claimed to have delivered bags of cash to the Vice President, her brother, Davao Rep. Paulo Duterte, and their father, then President Rodrigo Duterte.
Sara Duterte, in a news conference, presented evidence that Gracioso was lying about the supposed deliveries of cash allegedly from then Speaker Lord Allan Velasco of Marinduque.
Paulo Duterte and Velasco have also denied Gracioso's allegations.
Duterte’s alleged properties

Matibag said that Duterte declared two properties in Catigan, Davao City. The acquisition cost was P890,000, but the assessed value was actually P40 million to P60 million. The improvements to the property were also not declared .

Davao restaurant Prime Bistro, named under Duterte’s husband lawyer Manases Carpio, was also declared on the Vice President’s SALN. The acquisition cost was declared at P10 million but the assessed value was P82,000. The restaurant has a building that cost around P4.5 million, with the land value being P9.5 million, yet the declared acquisition cost was only P10 million.
Duterte’s SALN also listed a property in Don Bosco, Parañaque. The property’s market value on her SALN was P240,000, yet the acquisition cost was P2.2 million and the building was P461,760.
“But when we had it assessed by the assessor, it was P14,400,000,” Matibag said in Filipino.

There was also property listed in Aundanao, whose acquisition was P9 million, yet the real assessment was P19.5 million. Matibag said that there were also several undeclared improvements to the property. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Elon Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – Europe live
articles.summary:
Ukraine president Zelenskyy said he felt ‘betrayed’ by the US after Trump’s diesel deal and the Starlink restrictions

As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions
Billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk has suggested that the US government could be behind the decision to restrict the speed of SpaceX’s satellite-technology used by Ukraine’s military.
In a post of X, he appeared to suggest the Trump administration was behind the move, which Ukraine says restricts its ability to use key defensive weapons.

blocks.caption: A Ukrainian serviceman of 47th brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet systems at his positions at a front line. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Musk said:

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

In further posts overnight, reacting to Zelenskyy’s comments on his relationship with Donald Trump, Musk went further and appeared to suggest Zelenskyy should leave the post, saying it’s “time to go.”
In a TV interview with Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decisions and worried about “losing a strong partner,” playing a critical role across Ukraine’s defence.

For what it’s worth, Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The issue is likely to come up again today and tomorrow as EU leaders meet in Brussels for key political talks on the future.

With today’s discussions focused on the bloc’s internal matters, including the EU’s next budget, Ukraine is expected to come up on Friday when Zelenskyy joins other leaders in Brussels. But the ongoing crisis in Ukraine’s relations with the US risks overshadowing the entire meeting.
I will bring you all the updates throughout the day.
It’s Thursday, 15 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 11m agoStarlink satellite restrictions highlight Europe's dependency on US technology
15m agoMorning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions

blocks.text: Starlink satellite restrictions highlight Europe's dependency on US technology

As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer ⁠any ready-made alternatives, Reuters reported.

blocks.caption: A Starlink satellite internet system is set up near the frontline town of Bakhmut amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, Donetsk region. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters

blocks.text: European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelenskyy. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily ‌on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.

Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Wednesday following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by ‌investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.

Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.

It will be alleged the accused and the victim were in a personal relationship.
Detectives arrested the 43-year-old woman last week.

articles.title: NBI: Findings on Duterte couple’s SALNs based on signed documents, not gossip
articles.summary: NBI Director Melvin Matibag emphasized that the bureau's findings were not gossip but were based on documents signed by the couple.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 3:45pm
Composite image shows Vice President Sara Duterte as seen in June 2026 and her husband, Mans Carpio, in April 2026.
Duterte office; The STAR / Miguel de Guzman; Philstar.com composite

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has clarified that its findings regarding the alleged discrepancies in the Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, are based strictly on official documents signed and submitted by the couple themselves.
In a press conference on Thursday, October 15, NBI Director Melvin Matibag emphasized that the bureau's findings were not gossip but were based on documents signed by the couple.

“Hindi ito marites, hindi chismis, dahil dokumento yung nagsasalita at sila ang nakapirma sa dokumento parehas abogado si Attorney Man Carpio at si Vice President Sara Duterte with a grade of 80% of our exam,” Matibag said.

(This is not gossip or hearsay, because the documents speak for themselves, and they are the ones who signed the documents. Both Attorney Man Carpio and Vice President Sara Duterte are lawyers, with a grade of 80% in our exam.)
Among the key properties highlighted by the NBI is the "Prime Bistro," which is registered under Carpio's name.
According to the NBI, the couple’s SALN declares an acquisition cost of P10 million for the Prime Bistro.
However, the declared fair market value and assessed value of the property were listed at only P82,000.
Matibag said there was a clear conflict in these figures, pointing out that the estimated value of the land was P9.5 million, with an additional building on the site costing P4.5 million.

The NBI chief added that the bureau conducted its verification by obtaining Transfer Certificates of Title (TCTs) from the Land Registration Authority, visiting the physical locations, utilizing geotagging technology, and interviewing local residents.
Addressing the vice president's denial of owning some of these properties, Matibag questioned why they were explicitly declared in her SALN in the first place.
“Ang pinakamalinaw po rito that is a self-declaration ng SALN nila naka-describe nakalagay 'yung TCT number, nakalagay kung kailan na-acquire, bumabangga do'n sa TCT,” Matibag said.
(The clearest point here is that this is their own self-declared SALN—it describes and lists the TCT number and indicates when it was acquired—and it directly conflicts with the TCT records.)
“Sila po nagdeklara nito. Hindi po namin ginawa 'tong ebidensya na'to. Sila na po mismo ang nagbigay,” he added.
(They were the ones who declared this. We did not manufacture this evidence—they provided it themselves.)
The NBI forwarded its initial findings, consisting of a 178-page report, to the Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday, October 14, for appropriate action.

The NBI referrals involve two separate matters: alleged SALN misdeclarations involving properties linked to Duterte, which the bureau sent to the Office of the Ombudsman, and alleged flood-control project irregularities involving Genesis88 Construction, which it sent to the Department of Justice.
The central allegation is that Duterte misdeclared or underdeclared property values and improvements.

One property the NBI highlighted consists of lots declared as “agricultural lots” in Barangay Catigan, Davao City, which were listed in her SALN at a combined P890,000 but which the NBI estimated to be worth P40.72 million to P61.08 million based on inspections and initial valuations.

articles.title: New DICT chief faces task of putting house in order amid digital ambitions
articles.summary: Robert Joseph de Claro inherits a department beset by procurement controversies, internal disputes, and questions over its ability to deliver essential digital services

blocks.text: ROBERT DE CLARO. The new DICT chief attends a briefing at the DICT office, Wednesday, October 14, 2026
DICT
Robert Joseph de Claro inherits a department beset by procurement controversies, internal disputes, and questions over its ability to deliver essential digital services

items: The newly appointed DICT Secretary Robert Joseph de Claro faces the challenge of addressing internal controversies and improving the agency's management of public resources.
De Claro has committed to a comprehensive review of the DICT's projects and budgets within three months, amid scrutiny over past financial management and operational issues.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines — As the Philippines races to modernize government services, improve internet connectivity, and position itself for the age of artificial intelligence (AI), the agency tasked with leading that transformation faces a more immediate challenge: putting its own house in order.

This is the situation that newly appointed Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) Secretary Robert Joseph de Claro faces. The former Social Security System (SSS) chief replaced Henry Aguda following a tumultuous tenure marked by budget controversies, internal disagreements reported in the media, and questions over the implementation of government technology projects.

De Claro has promised a comprehensive review of the department’s projects, budgets, and procurement processes, with a clearer plan for the agency, BusinessMirror reported. Give him 3 months, he told reporters.
The commitment comes as the DICT faces mounting pressure to demonstrate that it can effectively manage public resources while delivering on the administration’s digitalization goals.

Questions over the department’s financial management surfaced as early as late 2025, when DICT officials disclosed that its budget contained P8.3 billion in excess funds, compared to what they had originally proposed under the National Expenditure Program.
Officials at the time said P5 billion had been used for connectivity initiatives, including the Bayanihan SIM program and free Wi-Fi for schools, while P3.3 billion was not released to the agency.

Then-undersecretary Christina Faye Condez-de Sagon rejected allegations linking her to questionable budget insertions. De Sagon said, “… we were a disruptive force in DICT. We brought in a new kind of leadership, we brought in better governance, I believe,” in an ABS-CBN report.

In hindsight, these were already probably murmurs of trouble in paradise because in August 2026, Malacanang would dismiss Condez-de Sagon, and assistant secretary June Vincent Manuel Gaudan over alleged procurement violations.

In December 2025 as well, Rappler uncovered internal DICT audits that alleged eGov Undersecretary David Almirol Jr. had conflict of interest issues arising from contracts between the agency and companies he formerly had ties with. A separate audit also warned of the possible weak data protections due to the absence of contracts in the implementation of the eGov app together with partner local governments.
Later in April 2026, the agency once again faced scrutiny over the reliability of its digital services.

A two-day outage of the eGovPH app exposed infrastructure and funding constraints after a surge in users overwhelmed systems. At a Senate hearing, Senator Bam Aquino said, “You need to subscribe to a higher tier. Usually, you just pay — and that solves your problem,” referring to scalable cloud infrastructure. “Clearly, that’s not acceptable,” Aquino reprimanded the agency.

Internal disagreements further complicated matters. In May, BusinessMirror reported that two information technology organizations warned that tensions between Aguda and Almirol Jr. could undermine public services and the country’s digital transformation agenda, and called for cooperation between the two.

In September, the Office of the Ombudsman announced a fact-finding investigation into alleged “ghost internet” projects involving the agency’s flagship Free Wifi For All initiative, including possible payments for undelivered services and the use of substandard or counterfeit software.

That same month, the House also deferred its proposed budget due to concerns over the supposed lack of results in online safety, particularly in the wake of the multiple fatal school shootings in the second half of the year, with supposed ties to online entities influencing the youth to commit violent acts or nihilistic violent extremism.
Aguda’s final weeks were marked by backlash over the DICT’s temporary blocking of Discord, a decision reversed within a day.

In an odd incident, the DICT retracted its statement that the House had invited Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to a hearing, blaming news organizations for spreading the information, even if it came from its own Facebook page itself. A mere error? Or a sign of internal turmoil surfacing?
Now, for de Claro, the challenge extends beyond resolving the controversies he inherited.
The DICT must simultaneously expand public connectivity, strengthen cybersecurity, maintain digital government platforms, and establish policies for emerging technologies — its known mandates.

But first, these ambitions will require institutional stability, and regaining the public confidence in the agency’s ability to deliver after a year of tumult. For an agency central to the Philippines’ digital future, rebuilding confidence in its own operations by sorting out whatever factions that have formed in the past year may be the first step toward fulfilling that mandate.
And after that, can new leadership demonstrate that existing programs are properly funded, implemented, and monitored? De Claro has 3 months to get this started on the right foot. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian denies 2027 budget 'dangled' before senator-judges for VP Sara conviction vote
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Thursday refuted claims that the 2027 national budget is being dangled before senator-judges in order to secure votes for the conviction of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published October 15, 2026 3:33pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Thursday refuted claims that the 2027 national budget is being dangled before senator-judges in order to secure votes for the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.

In an ambush interview, Gatchalian said there is “no basis” to the allegations that the 2027 budget is being used to pressure senator-judges or is being offered to them as some sort of reward in exchange for their vote to convict the Vice President.
“Walang gano’n. Walang gano’n na dina-dangle sa senator or senator-judges,” the Senate President said.
(There’s nothing like that. Nothing is being dangled before the senators or the senator-judges.)

“First, kaka-transmit lang sa amin ‘yung budget last Monday. So, nag-umpisa pa lang pinag-aaralan ‘yung budget, although meron na kaming mga advanced studies… So ngayon pa lang namin hinihimay. Since ngayon pa lang hinihimay, so wala pa kaming ginagalaw sa budget,” he explained.

(First, the budget was only transmitted to us last Monday. So, we have just begun studying it, although we already had some preliminary studies. But we are only going through it now in detail. Since we are still in the process of scrutinizing it, we haven’t made any changes to the budget yet.)
On Wednesday, Vice President Sara Duterte said the people would be taken for granted, if the impeachment and the national budget are being used “as instruments of political survival of the corrupt.”

“If impeachment and the national budget are being used as instruments of political survival of the corrupt, then it is the people, not the defense counsel, who are being taken for granted,” Duterte said as she defended lead defense counsel, Atty. Sheila Sison, from accusation of being a “bully” in the impeachment trial.
Senate impeachment court’s credibility
Gatchalian said the credibility of the Senate impeachment court may be compromised because of such claims, but he assured that the judgment of the senator-judges would be “impartial and fair.”
“In fact, hindi in any way konektado ‘yung budget sa magiging judgment ng impeachment. Ang direction ng impeachment is to render impartial and fair judgment,” he said.
(In fact, the budget is in no way connected to our judgment in the impeachment case. The direction of the impeachment proceedings is to deliver an impartial and fair judgment.)
Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate Committee on Finance, confirmed Wednesday that the Senate already received the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB) from the House of Representatives.
He, however, questioned the reported realignment of around P206 billion in the House’s version of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Indian woman and boyfriend get death sentence in 'blue drum' murder case
articles.summary: The body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains details that some readers may find distressing.
A woman and her boyfriend have been sentenced to death for the murder of her husband in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
Muskan Rastogi, 26, and Sahil Shukla, 28, were convicted on 30 September by a court in Meerut city for the 2025 murder of her husband Saurabh Rajput.
Rajput's body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum - leading to the case being dubbed as "the blue drum murder".
Wednesday's death sentences have to be confirmed by the high court. Rastogi and Shukla have the option to challenge the verdict.
The prosecution said in court that Rastogi and Shukla had been classmates in school and had grown close in the absence of Rajput who worked in London.
When Rajput first came to know of their affair in 2021, he had wanted to get a divorce but was persuaded against this by his family since the couple had a young daughter.
Rajput was murdered on 3 March 2025 when he was visiting Meerut. Police said he was given food laced with sedatives by Rastogi before he was killed.
Rastogi and Shukla fled to Himachal Pradesh state but used Rajput's mobile phone to send text messages to his family to make it seem like he was alive and travelling for business, they added.
A few days later, however, Rajput's family lodged a complaint with the police saying that he was missing.
On 17 March, when Rastogi visited her parents after returning from Himachal Pradesh, her six-year-old daughter asked about her father.
Rastogi initially blamed her in-laws for her husband's murder. Unconvinced, her parental family took her to the police station.
Rastogi confessed to the crime during interrogation and she and Shukla were arrested and charged with the murder.
"My brother was killed by cruel people," Rajput's brother told BBC Hindi.
Rastogi's parents also demanded strict action against her.
"My daughter, along with a friend, murdered her husband in her own home. She is not fit for this society and is a danger to others," her father told ANI news agency.
Rastogi gave birth to a second child while in jail.

October 15, 2026
Three Indians killed in Germany building fire, arson suspected
Three Indian nationals were killed in a fire at an apartment building in western Germany's Bochum.
The Indian Embassy in Berlin said in a statement that two women and one man were among those who died, adding that all three were studying in Germany.
According to German media reports, the victims were aged between 25 and 27. Five other people were injured.

German news agency DPA said that the fire department received an alert at 4:15 a.m. local time (0212 GMT/UTC). Residents were seen calling for help as they stood at windows on the first and second floors of the building, DPA reported.
The firefighting efforts lasted several hours.
A technical malfunction was ruled out as the cause of the fire and authorities said they were investigating a suspected arson.
A 41-year-old man, who is a resident of the building, has been arrested on suspicion of murder and is in pretrial detention, reports said citing a police statement.
The reports identified the man as a Romanian national.
Meanwhile, the Indian Embassy said it was in touch with German authorities and the families of the victims. It added that it was offering all necessary assistance.
"We extend our deepest condolences to the bereaved families in this hour of grief," the statement from the embassy said.
Bochum's mayor, Jörg Lukat, called the incident a "tragedy the likes of which Bochum has not seen in decades."

articles.title: [Pastilan] Sara wants to answer? Start with the wealth
articles.summary: So who is behind Sara’s problems? Sara, chiefly. If all that documented wealth was not declared in her SALNs, she has no one but herself to thank for the questions it raises.

blocks.text: So who is behind Sara’s problems? Sara, chiefly. If all that documented wealth was not declared in her SALNs, she has no one but herself to thank for the questions it raises.

items: Sara Duterte's defenders have expressed outrage over the withdrawal of three impeachment articles, but their previous lack of transparency raises questions about their sincerity.

The prosecution's decision to focus on a single article of impeachment regarding unexplained wealth has narrowed the case, yet substantial financial evidence remains unaddressed by Duterte and her legal team.

Despite the change in prosecution strategy, the essential questions about the source of Duterte's wealth and financial discrepancies persist, necessitating a clear response from her to uphold public accountability.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

There is something unconvincing about Sara Duterte and her defenders suddenly discovering the virtues of a full and fair hearing after prosecutors withdrew three of the four articles of impeachment against the Vice President this week.

The complaint is not entirely without merit. The prosecution spent over a month presenting evidence on grave threats and the alleged misuse of confidential funds, only to abandon those charges, including the one on bribery, after it was done with its case on unexplained wealth.

Articles 1, 3, and 4 are gone, leaving Article 2 to carry the entire burden. What looked like a broad prosecution has become a concentrated gamble. The prosecutors have narrowed their battlefield and staked their chances of conviction on a single front.

blocks.caption: Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Sara, who benefits?

blocks.text: It is possible to question the wisdom of this decision without pretending that it constitutes some monumental injustice. Lawyers are entitled to decide which charges they believe could get the job done. The objective of a prosecution is not to accumulate the largest number of accusations, like stamps in a passport, but to secure a conviction. Al Capone was not undone by a full catalogue of his crimes but by tax evasion. Sometimes, it can only take one to do someone in.
But what is hard to stomach is the sudden eruption of indignation from a camp that has spent some time behaving as though the very act of asking questions was an intolerable persecution.

Where was this appetite for giving answers before the impeachment trial? Where was it during the House hearings? Where was it when Sara Duterte was repeatedly asked to explain her finances and responded with verbal evasion? Her celebrated answer, “shimenet,” was not an explanation. It was a noise made in place of one.

Sara has perfected the art of substituting grievance for argument. She presents herself as the victim of political persecution, accuses her critics of malice, and wraps herself in the familiar costume of the embattled underdog. Her defenders dutifully repeat the performance.
Yet the essential questions remain stubbornly unanswered. Where did the money come from, where did it go, and why do the figures appear so difficult to reconcile?

When her lawyers were pressed during the early weeks of the impeachment trial, their refrain was that they would answer “at the proper time.” One might wonder whether this proper time belongs to the same category as the mythical land of milk and honey, forever promised but never reached.

Now that prosecutors have withdrawn three of the four articles, the defense has discovered a fresh cause for outrage. Its leader has lambasted the prosecution, as though the abandonment of charges were an assault on the accused rather than a tactical decision by the accusers. Did I get it right that they want four instead of one charge against their client, or was it just to feed the Duterte trolls?

One is also tempted to wonder whether the outburst has anything to do with the consequences of a shorter trial, including fewer appearances and potentially lower lawyers’ appearance fees. As I watched the defense lawyer throw a tantrum, one sentence kept playing at the back of my head: “Your Honor, we respectfully appeal this decision on financial grounds.”

That is speculation, of course, and should not be mistaken for an established motive. But the spasm of indignation did invite an uncomfortable question about who benefits from dragging proceedings out.

The withdrawal may also have upset the Duterte camp‘s apparent penchant for delay. A defense that had contemplated presenting more than 90 witnesses might now find that the stage has become considerably smaller.

This brings to mind Sara’s own advice about the need for a Plan A, Plan B, and Plan C. Applied to this situation, it is sound advice, though rather less impressive coming from someone whose political survival increasingly depends on never having to explain herself. One wonders what comes after indignation, evasion and the familiar claim of persecution. Is there a Plan D, or does the alphabet run out before the excuses do?

What is done is done. The prosecution has made its decision, and the impeachment court has accepted the withdrawal. The remaining business is therefore quite straightforward. Sara and her lawyers should answer the allegations that remain, rather than continue to manufacture distractions around the manner in which the case is being prosecuted.

The unexplained wealth allegations cannot simply be waved away as fabrications. The prosecution has presented financial documents and called witnesses from the Office of the Ombudsman, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System, the Anti-Money Laundering Council, the Bureau of Internal Revenue, banks and insurance companies. A financial forensic analyst has also presented his findings. They are substantial enough to merit answers.
It is difficult to imagine why all those bankers would lie, and how they could possibly have managed to do so in concert. And the figures are not difficult to understand.

items: Sara’s declared net worth rose from P7.2 million in 2007 to P98.6 million in 2025.

Even when she was already Vice President, she did not divest and retained a stake in at Metro City Chow Foods Corporation and Gencorp Industries Incorporated, a firm which secured Davao City government contracts worth P34.2 million. Her brother, Mayor Baste Duterte, claimed he did not know Sara had interests in the firm even as he said that he merely appointed a representative to sign the contracts.

Authorities also reported P4.4 billion in covered and suspicious transactions linked to Sara and her husband between 2007 and 2025, including P319 million in remittances from China to Cale88 Foods Corporation. Later, Sara asked whether it was wrong to do business with Chinese firms, stopping just short of admitting what the question plainly invited her to confront. If one happens to be the vice president, the answer is yes.

The proceedings examined properties linked to her husband, 19 insurance policies, and questions about Sara’s compensation income and constitutional restrictions on outside employment. The BIR cited records showing she received compensation from the Davao City Hall even when was already getting paid as vice president. If it wasn’t double compensation, I don’t know what is.

On October 9, a financial forensic analyst reported over P817 million in allegedly undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025. He said the figure could reach P1.5 billion without his conservative assumptions, citing discrepancies between companies’ declared capital and earnings and the extent of alleged under-reporting.

blocks.text: Let’s return to the question: Was all this wealth declared in her SALNs? Did she disclose the full extent of her wealth? Given the documented figures, “persecution” hardly qualifies as a financial explanation.

If the figures are wrong, identify the errors. If the assets were lawfully acquired, explain their source. If the properties and income were properly declared, produce the records. If the companies’ accounts have been misread, demonstrate how. The defense has every right to dismantle the prosecution’s case, but it must do so with something more substantial than indignation.

Sara is entitled to answer, and answer she should. What she is not entitled to is the presumption that demanding answers from her constitutes an act of political persecution. Public office comes with obligations, and declaring one’s assets is not an optional exercise.

The withdrawal of three impeachment articles may have changed the prosecution’s strategy, but it did not magically resolve the questions raised by the financial evidence. The point is to establish the facts, not to award victory to whichever camp shouts loudest.

Sara has told people to always have a back-up plan. Perhaps it is time to try a more radical proposition. Go to the impeachment court, answer the questions, produce the documents, and let the evidence speak pertaining to the unexplained wealth charge.
She wants to answer? Then answer she must. Pastilan. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ADF member ‘person of interest’ after video recorder found in HMAS Leeuwin women’s showers
articles.summary:
Vice Admiral Buckley calls incident an ‘act of sexual violence’ and a ‘despicable betrayal of trust’

The defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of…

blocks.text: The defence department says a member of the Australian Defence Force is a “person of interest” in investigations after a video recording device was found in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin, in what the chief of Navy called a “despicable betrayal of trust”.

A day after senator Jacqui Lambie told the Senate that a hidden camera had been found in a female shower facility onboard the naval ship, docked in Cairns, navy chief Matt Buckley confirmed a “video recording device” had been located in one of the ship’s bathrooms.

In a statement, Vice Admiral Buckley called the incident an “act of sexual violence” and “the most despicable betrayal of trust”, and said the navy was conducting a review of all bathrooms across the service.

Defence confirmed on Wednesday that a “video recording device” was found in the cabin of the vessel, which it had referred to the Joint Military Police Unit. It came hours after Lambie – an ADF veteran and advocate for defence personnel – told the Senate she’d been contacted by a former member of the navy with allegations about a camera being found aboard HMAS Leeuwin.
Defence did not initially confirm where the device had been found, or any details about its investigation.
On Thursday, the department gave a further update.

“An Australian Defence Force member has been identified as a person of interest in the investigation into a video recording device being located on Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin,” the department said.
“This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its enquiries. Navy’s focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident.”
In a written statement, Buckley informed Navy members of the update.
“I consider this a most serious matter, and accordingly, the Ship’s program has been altered to enable a rapid and rigorous investigation by the Joint Military Policing Unit,” he wrote.
“My highest priority, as always, is the wellbeing of our people.”
Buckley said the Navy was conducting a “100% audit of all of our bathrooms across the Fleet”.
“This act is the most despicable betrayal of trust and is fundamentally misaligned with our values,” he said.

“You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy. Any perpetrator will be held to account. Further, you should all know that eradicating sexual violence in our workplace is fundamental to the fighting efficiency of our Navy. I invite all of you to make this your priority.”

The defence minister, Richard Marles, described the incident as “reprehensible, invasive and is the most despicable breach of trust.” He said he was receiving updates on the investigation as it continued.
“There is no place for this behaviour in the Australian Defence Force. Our priority remains supporting the individuals who have been impacted,” he said in a statement on social media on Thursday.
On Wednesday, Lambie asked whether images captured by the device had been published online.

“How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask Navy,” she said.
Buckley said “all potentially impacted personnel are receiving our strongest support”, adding that the warrant officer of the navy was in Cairns to support the ship’s company.

articles.title: Pulse Asia: Marcos' trust, approval ratings slightly up; Sara Duterte's slip
articles.summary: The trust and approval ratings of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. rose slightly, while Vice President Sara Duterte's counterpart numbers declined in September 2026, a survey of Pulse Asia…
articles.byline: GISELLE OMBAY, MARIEL CELINE SERQUIÑA, GMA News

blocks.text: SEPTEMBER 2026 SURVEY
Published October 15, 2026 2:58pm

The trust and approval ratings of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. rose slightly, while Vice President Sara Duterte's counterpart numbers declined in September 2026, a survey of Pulse Asia Research Inc. showed Thursday.

The survey, conducted from September 17 to 24, 2026, found that Marcos' approval and trust ratings both climbed 1 percentage point to 30% and 29%, respectively. These were improvements compared to the previous survey conducted in July 2026.
As for Duterte, her approval rating slid 2 percentage points to 54%, while her trust rating decreased by 3 percentage points to 55%.
Overall, Duterte maintained the appreciation and trust of most adult Filipinos.

"Small majorities continue to approve of the Vice-President's performance (54%) and trust her (55%) while near majorities are critical of the President's work (49%) and express distrust in him (48%)," Pulse Asia reported.

blocks.caption: Courtesy: Pulse Asia

blocks.text: Courtesy: Pulse Asia
Nearly half of Filipino adults, or 48%, were found to distrust Marcos. Only 29% showed big trust in him, while 22% were undecided.

Trust in the President was highest in Balance Luzon (43%), and among Class ABC (33%) and Class D (30%). However, distrust was evident in Mindanao (66%) and Visayas (60%), as well as those in Class E (55%).
On the other hand, Duterte enjoyed the most trust from adults at 55%, with 27% having small or no trust at all, and 19% being unsure.
The vice president had the most trust in Mindanao (94%) and among Class E (69%). Her distrust was highest in the National Capital Region (41%) and among Class D (28%) and Class ABC (27%).
Compared to July 2026, the September 2026 survey showed that Marcos' disapproval rating slightly dipped by 3 percentage points.
Notably, Pulse Asia's survey showed that from July 2026, Marcos experienced a drop in his distrust ratings in Mindanao (-11 percentage points) and Class ABC (-16 percentage points) in September 2026.
The ambivalence toward the President's trustworthiness also became more manifest in Mindanao (+11 percentage points).
On the other hand, Duterte had a 3-percentage point decrease in trust ratings, and no changes in distrust ratings.
Pulse Asia said the only significant change in the vice president's trustworthiness figures was the decline in trust in Class D by losing 5 percentage points.

blocks.caption: Courtesy: Pulse Asia

blocks.text: Performance ratings

When it comes to performance, the survey showed that more Filipinos (49%) disapproved of the work done by Marcos in the past quarter, as compared to those who approved it at 30%. There were 21% who were also undecided.
The majority, meanwhile, continued to appreciate Duterte's work (54%), as compared to 27% who disapproved and 18% who are ambivalent.
Approval of the President's performance was highest in Balance Luzon (42%) and among Class ABC (37%), while that of the Vice President was highest in Mindanao (91%) and Class E (68%).

In Class ABC, approval for Marcos’ performance became more marked with +17 percentage points, while his disapproval eased by -19 percentage points. Disapproval for the President’s work was also more evident in Class E with +14 percentage points.
As for the Vice President, indecision as to approving or disapproving her performance was more notable (+5 percentage points).
The survey used face-to-face interviews, with a sample of 2,400 adults 18 years old and above.
It has a ± 2% error margin at 95% confidence level, and has ± 4% error margin at 95% confidence level specifically for Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. — VDV, GMA News
