articles.title: Politician from Mindanao financed flight for drug shipment from Laos — PDEA
articles.summary: The agency has not revealed the identity of the politician, but said that it provided the P3.5 billion payment for the chartered private jet.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 2:52pm
This screenshot from Google Maps shows the Mindanao region, October 15, 2026.
Google Maps / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) said on Thursday, October 15, that a politician from Mindanao has allegedly funded the flight that was meant to deliver the drug shipment from Laos.

The agency has not revealed the identity of the politician, but said that it provided the P3.5 billion payment for the chartered private jet that was supposed to carry 521 kilograms of suspected methamphetamine or shabu to the country, according to a report by The STAR.

Lao authorities intercepted the supposed drug shipment at Luang Prabang International Airport in Laos after the pilot of the private jet reportedly refused to load the luggage of alias “Fajad,” a confirmed Filipino national, who was allegedly carrying the suspected drugs.
PDEA also identified another Filipino named alias “Boyet” who allegedly arranged the flight.
Fajad was reportedly arrested and detained in Laos, while authorities say Boyet has left the country since October 10.
The agency has earlier said that they have already identified the mastermind behind the attempted drug smuggling, but refused to release more details to avoid compromising the ongoing investigation.
According to the agency, both Boyet and Fajad have alleged links to the major drug syndicate Sam Gor responsible for distributing illegal drugs across Asia-Pacific.
The syndicate has an alleged wide influence in Mindanao because it uses the region as an entry point to the Philippines, PDEA added.

articles.title: Marcos joins world leaders' prayers, support for Pope Leo after surgery
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has joined other world leaders in expressing support for Pope Leo XIV following a surgery that removed a cancerous lung nodule from the pontiff.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 2:46pm
View of a small altar displaying a photograph of Pope Leo XIV, at a house in Chiclayo, Lambayeque department, northern Peru, on October 11, 2026.
AFP / Ernesto Benavides
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has joined other world leaders in expressing support for Pope Leo XIV following a surgery that removed a cancerous lung nodule from the pontiff.
"The entire Filipino nation joins the Catholic faithful around the world in praying for the swift and full recovery of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV," Marcos said in a statement on Thursday, October 15.
Marcos expressed that he was looking forward to the pope's "return to good health" and "to his continued spiritual leadership, guidance and blessings for the faithful."
Leo underwent lung surgery Tuesday, October 13 and is expected to remain in the hospital for a week as part of his post-operation recovery, according to the Vatican's bulletin to the press.
The operation, a minimally invasive thoracic surgery, was completed "successfully," the Vatican said. The surgery removed the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, where a localized nodule was found.
Further examination of the removed nodule confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma (early-stage lung cancer).
The Pope is now awaiting the results of a biopsy to determine if the cancer has spread.
In an Angelus on Sunday, October 11, Leo announced he was undergoing surgery to remove a "localized nodule in my lung," noting that it is at "a very early stage."
Given the nodule was removed at an early stage, experts, including oncologists, have indicated that Leo's prognosis will likely be excellent.
In the meantime, clergy and members of the Vatican hierarchy have urged the public to continue to pray for the Pope.

At least 3,000 prayers and expressions of support have come from the Philippines in the online global "spiritual bouquet" being collated by the Order of St. Augustine for Leo, who served as prior general of the order from 2001 to 2010. — with reports from AFP

articles.title: EU summit to focus on China, Ukraine and bloc budget
articles.summary: EU leaders meeting in Brussels will examine measures to curb the bloc's huge trade deficit with China. But they will also be looking to further agreement on the next EU budget ahead of some major…

image.caption: The EU is holding a summit as the bloc faces rising economic challengesImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Union leaders are to meet in Brussels on Thursday for two days of talks that will focus on some of the major economic challenges facing the bloc, including competition from China.
The meeting is also likely to see some heated debate over the bloc's budget for the years 2028 to 2034, with the usual divisive negotiations between net contributors and net recipients.
On Friday, leaders are set to discuss further support for Ukraine as it faces a full-scale Russian invasion, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy due to attend.
Here are the main topics on the agenda:
Chinese competition in focus
The leaders are expected to discuss ways to remedy the bloc's massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.
The meeting comes less than a week after the bloc's executive body, the European Commission, reached an agreement with Beijing to curb imports of hybrid cars from China.
The EU has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field.
Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.
Ahead of the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron called for new EU measures to counter any actions leading to market distortion.
The leaders will, however, also be looking at soaring energy prices within the bloc as another factor weighing on its competitiveness.
Divisive EU budget
The bloc's next seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 is also set to be another controversial issue on the agenda, ahead of a special summit set for November to try to reach agreement.
Discussions on the budget, which requires unanimous approval, are often intense, with divisions between wealthier states and those that rely on EU cohesion funds.
The talks at the summit are not expected to bring any breakthrough, but leaders are hoping to reach a compromise by the end of the year.
Pressure to finalize the budget is growing ahead of elections next year in several member states that could make it even more difficult to reach a deal acceptable to all.
Ukraine support
The EU leaders are expected to turn their attention to the situation in Ukraine on Friday, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy invited to join the meeting.
He is likely to urge the bloc to up its support for Kyiv as Russia intensifies its strikes ahead of winter, killing dozens of civilians.

European aid is taking on ever more importance as the US under President Donald Trump continues its ambivalent path with regard to the conflict, as reflected in a recent deal securing Russian diesel imports despite international sanctions.
Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukrainian leader.

articles.title: Doctors treating Elizabeth Struhs recommended involuntary mental health assessment of her mother, coroner hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into death of Queensland girl denied insulin by her religious parents is told Kerrie Struhs believed God would heal her daughter

  • Get our

blocks.text: Doctors were so concerned about the religious beliefs of Elizabeth Struhs’ mother they recommended she be subjected to an involuntary mental health assessment because she delusionally believed her daughter would be healed from type 1 diabetes, a coroner has heard.
Child safety officers, nonetheless, decided to return the eight-year-old home to live with her mother, Kerrie Struhs, over the objections of Brisbane-based doctors, in 2019.

Elizabeth died on 7 January 2022, at her home in Rangeville, Toowoomba, after her insulin was stopped by her father, Jason Struhs. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.
The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence from three child safety officers involved in Elizabeth’s case on Thursday.

Elizabeth came to the attention of the department of child safety in 2019 after she was hospitalised with late-stage diabetic ketoacidosis on 17 July, a potentially fatal ailment that affects people with type 1 diabetes who are not given insulin. The court has heard she was so unwell she was in a coma and nearly died.
Despite her poor condition, Kerrie objected to Jason driving her to hospital, believing Elizabeth would be miraculously healed.
Kerrie later participated in an interview involving child safety officers and health staff.
Contemporaneous notes taken from the meeting presented in court read: “Kerrie stated that Elizabeth cannot keep this disease and she will be healed.
“(A health) consultant stated that they have treated 100s of children and parents and no one has ever reverted back from the diabetes or got rid of type 1,” the notes read.
“Kerrie stated that she has to trust in God to heal Elizabeth as God promised her he will hear her.”
A consultant asked Kerrie what she would do if she was home with Elizabeth and her sugar levels dropped, a sign of health risk.
“Kerrie stated that she will pray straight away,” the notes read.

The coroner has heard that doctors based in Brisbane repeatedly urged child safety officers not to return her home due to her religious beliefs, which they deemed “delusional”, but one told the court on Monday she felt “stonewalled” by them.
Notes of a phone call she made at the time were presented in court on Thursday.
“Child safety officer explained that the mother would not engage in any mental health assessments if recommended given her beliefs,” a child safety officer told her.
after newsletter promotion
“(The doctor) stated that this is why they believe she requires an involuntary assessment and that child safety could arrange this.”
Both parents were later convicted of failing to provide the necessities of life as a result of delaying seeking medical help during the incident, with Kerrie jailed.
Child safety officers decided to return her home into the care of her father, which they did in August.

They developed a safety plan for Elizabeth and had her parents sign an intervention with parental agreement – a form of voluntary arrangement to keep a child safe at home without needing a court-ordered custody or guardianship arrangement.
The document, which was presented in court, laid out the expectations the department had for Elizabeth’s parents.

It said child safety was “worried” that Kerrie and her other children would convince Elizabeth that she was “healed by God … which could lead to Elizabeth refusing to take her medication making her very sick or putting her at risk of death”.
Jason promised to provide insulin to his daughter and did so for two years, before he was convinced to stop by other members of the sect – known as the Saints – in 2021.
All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Supreme Court: Senior citizen discount can't be combined with promos
articles.summary: In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the High Court reversed lower-court rulings that found Orville Ong guilty of violating Republic Act (R.A.) No. 7432, as amended by Republic Act No. 9994 or…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 2:32pm
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has acquitted a Bacolod City hotel general manager charged with violating the Senior Citizens Act, ruling that statutory elderly discounts cannot be combined with existing promotional or group-negotiated rates.

In a statement on Wednesday, October 14, the high court reversed lower court rulings that found Orville Ong guilty of violating Republic Act No. 7432, as amended by Republic Act No. 9994, or the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010.
Ong was charged after hotel guests, lawyer Paul S. Alcazaren, 66, and Eric Gadiana, 70, were denied an additional 20% senior citizen discount on their room accommodations.
Ong contended that the hotel had already extended a 20% discount on the room rates negotiated for members of the Cebu Bikers Club, to which both guests belonged.
Although the deduction was integrated into the total lump sum rather than itemized separately on the official receipt, Ong argued that the discount had already been fully applied.

While the Municipal Trial Court in Cities, the Regional Trial Court, and the Court of Appeals had all previously sustained Ong's conviction, the Supreme Court ruled in his favor, clarifying that the hotel was under no obligation to grant a second 20% markdown.
Clarifying the framework governing senior citizens' benefits, the Supreme Court emphasized that senior citizen discounts cannot be stacked on top of other promotional offers.

Under existing regulations, when goods or services are offered at promotional or discounted rates, senior citizens can choose either the promotional rate or the statutory 20% senior citizen discount, whichever yields greater savings.
However, businesses are not mandated to enforce both simultaneously.
"Granting an additional discount beyond what the law allows would unfairly benefit the customer at the business’s expense," the Court noted in a press statement released Wednesday.
The Supreme Court stressed that statutory privileges must be enforced with fairness toward commercial establishments.

“The State’s pursuit of public welfare cannot be allowed to impose undue or confiscatory burdens on private establishments, whose continued viability is essential to the long-term effectiveness of the law,” the high court declared.

The ruling sets a precedent for hospitality, food and retail service providers nationwide, confirming that businesses fulfilling mandatory discount percentages through negotiated group rates or sales promotions are protected against claims of non-compliance under RA 9994.

articles.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
articles.summary: China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces.

blocks.text: A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties.
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.

The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.

A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."

Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.
But the alliance is not without tension.

Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.
China's attitude has shifted more recently.

"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.

At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte keeps majority trust ratings amid impeachment trial
articles.summary: So far, the surveys show that public trust in and approval of Duterte have defied expectations of a reputation-bruising trial, where allegations of Duterte's unexplained wealth and wanton use of…

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 2:10pm

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte continues to enjoy majority trust and approval ratings, according to two different surveys released this week, even as the Senate impeachment trial is now in full swing.

So far, the surveys show that public trust in and approval of Duterte have defied expectations of a reputation-bruising trial, where allegations of Duterte's unexplained wealth and wanton use of confidential fund have been heard.

Separate surveys released by Pulse Asia and Social Weather Stations (SWS) this week put Duterte's trust rating at 55% and 56%, respectively. In the Pulse Asia poll, 54% of Filipino adults also approved of her performance over the past quarter.
Pulse Asia's Ulat ng Bayan survey, conducted from September 17 to 24 through face-to-face interviews with 2,400 adults, found that 27% distrust the vice president while 19% were undecided.
On her performance, 27% disapproved and 18% could not say either way. The survey has a margin of error of ±2 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.
Duterte's ratings are virtually unchanged from Pulse Asia's July survey, when 58% said they trusted her and 56% approved of her work.
The only significant shift was among Class D respondents, where trust in her slipped five points to 53%.

On the other hand, the SWS survey, commissioned by Stratbase Institute, showed similarly steady numbers: 56% of Filipinos have "much trust" in Duterte, 26% have "little trust," and 17% are undecided, nearly identical to the 57%-27% split SWS recorded in June.
SWS conducted its survey from September 21 to 27.
Duterte's "much trust" rating in the SWS survey has stayed between 53% and 61% in every edition since March 2025, though it remains below the high 65% she posted in July 2024.
Mindanao bailiwick, split Luzon
Both surveys show Duterte's support remains anchored in Mindanao, her home region. Pulse Asia found 94% of Mindanawons trust her and 91% approve of her performance, with distrust at just 1%.
SWS recorded 87% "much trust" and only 4% "little trust" in the region.
Duterte also similarly holds majorities in the Visayas, with 57% trust in Pulse Asia's survey and 60% in SWS's, the latter up from 54% in June.
Luzon is more divided in perceptions of the vice president.
In Metro Manila, Pulse Asia found trust and distrust in Duterte nearly even at 43% and 41%, and her approval and disapproval tied at 42%.
In the rest of Luzon, trust stood at 37% against 38% distrust.
SWS shows Duterte has a wider edge in both areas: 46% much trust versus 33% little trust in Metro Manila, and 41% versus 35% in Balance Luzon.
Marcos underwater
The numbers stand in sharp contrast with those of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who remains well below the trust and approval ratings of Duterte.
In Pulse Asia's survey, nearly half of Filipinos disapproved of the president's performance (49%) and distrusted him (48%). Only 30% approved of his work, and 29% said they trust him.
Marcos failed to get majority approval in any geographic area or socioeconomic class, with disapproval reaching 71% in Mindanao and 66% in Class E, where it rose 14 points from July.
There were bright spots for the president in Class ABC, where his approval jumped 17 points to 37% and distrust fell 16 points. Distrust in him also eased in Mindanao, dropping 11 points to 66%.
SWS found a similar pattern, where Marcos' "much trust" rating was at 36% against 40% "little trust."
This is a slight improvement from June's 34%-45%. But it is also the fourth straight SWS survey since November 2025 in which more Filipinos expressed little trust than much trust in Marcos.
His rating has fallen from 64% in July 2024. In Mindanao, his "much trust" figure doubled from 17% in June to 35%.
Duterte's SWS trust rating has outpaced Marcos' in every survey since February 2025.
Trial backdrop
Pulse Asia's fieldwork overlapped with key developments in the impeachment trial. Throughout September, the prosecution focused on the confidential funds and unexplained wealth charge.
Earlier in the month, on September 5, Duterte was issued an arrest warrant for three counts of grave threats, charges that are also part of the impeachment case.
Duterte herself has not shown up to the impeachment trial and has not been called to take the witness stand.

The prosecution has also recently dropped its plan to call the vice president as a witness, with private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan telling reporters: "From what we heard from the defense, what she is going to say is that she knows nothing – that's all she is going to say in the witness stand."

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Comelec did not set barangay, SK polls for December 14
articles.summary: The Comelec flags a circulating graphic as fake. Under Republic Act No. 12326, the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections are scheduled for November 13, 2028.

blocks.text: Claim: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) announced that the next barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) would be held on December 14, 2026.
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post in the group “Duterte Legacy” that was published on October 8 carried the claim with a caption that reads, “Confirmed!”

The attached graphic mimics a Comelec announcement, displaying the poll body’s seal and the heading “Official Announcement.” It states: “This is to confirm the scheduled date for the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE). Despite any varying information, the scheduled date on record is December 14, 2026.”
Its text further states: “PAALALA: Ang opisyal na petsa ay maaaring magbago ayon sa batas. Manatiling nakatutok para sa anumang opisyal na bagong anunsyo mula sa COMELEC.”
(Reminder: The official date may change according to law. Stay tuned for any official new announcement from the Comelec.)
As of writing, the post had drawn 763 reactions, 136 comments, and 140 shares.

The facts: The Comelec did not announce a December 14 BSKE. On October 10, it warned the public that the circulating graphic was fake and urged the public to rely on the poll body’s official website and social media accounts for election-related announcements.

The graphic cites no law or Comelec resolution establishing December 14 as the election date. It provides no resolution number and merely directs readers to the Comelec website. The use of the poll body’s seal and official-looking design does not establish its authenticity.

Under Republic Act (RA) No. 12326, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on September 24, the next BSKE is scheduled for November 13, 2028. The law postponed the elections from the previous schedule of November 2, 2026.

Petitions before the Supreme Court seek to block the new law and compel the Comelec to hold the elections in 2026. The poll body has said that RA 12326 remains in effect because the Court has not issued a temporary restraining order.

Date change: The BSKE was initially scheduled for December 1, 2025. In August 2025, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed RA 12232, postponing the elections to November 2, 2026, and setting a four-year term for barangay and SK officials.
Senator Francis Escudero then filed Senate Bill No. 2387 in August 2026, seeking to extend the terms of barangay and SK officials from four to five years, amending RA 12232.

Escudero’s proposed measure was subsequently enacted as RA 12326. The law provides for elections every five years, on the second Monday of November, beginning in 2028. (READ: How often have barangay, SK elections been postponed?)

Fake dates: The shifting election schedules have fueled misinformation online. Rappler previously fact-checked a claim that the postponement had already become law before Marcos signed it, as well as another claiming that the elections would be held this coming November 28. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar, who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies from the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

items: Microsoft collaborated with Japan's National Police Agency and partners to dismantle a Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace responsible for phishing kits.
The operation targeted three components of the marketplace: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man, which collectively enabled over one billion malicious messages aimed at various organizations worldwide.
The phishing kits allowed criminals to impersonate trusted organizations, making it easier to execute phishing attacks across multiple sectors and countries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Microsoft worked with Japan’s National Police Agency and a host of partners, including cybersecurity companies and global nonprofit organization Health-ISAC, to dismantle part of the operations of a Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace responsible for creating and selling phishing kits — or accounts, hosting services and tools for building fake websites and online identities.
In an October 14 blog post, Microsoft said it and Health-ISAC dismantled three parts of that marketplace’s infrastructure: YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man.

Steven Masada, general counsel and general manager of Microsoft’s Digital Crimes Unit, said YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have since January 2026 “collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone.”

He added, “These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators.”

While YAM Store provided the infrastructure, the phishing kits sold on the marketplace, including CoGUI and Iron Man, provided bad actors with access to ready-made templates allowing them to impersonate trusted organizations. With the templates in hand, criminals could quickly send email, text and web content tailored to specific brands, industries, and countries in an effort to get people to click on phishing links.

Masada explained that the phishing kits allowed for impersonation attempts across a spectrum of organizations, from government agencies to banks, retailers, and parcel delivery services from various countries and in numerous languages.

Masada added, “YAM Store, CoGUI, and Iron Man are only part of that larger criminal network, but disrupting them makes it harder for criminals to obtain the accounts, tools and infrastructure they rely on.”
A more technical breakdown of the phishing infrastructure that complements the Microsoft blogpost is available on Microsoft’s security blog. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings still have no public outcome, BBC Verify finds
articles.summary: BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents from the past three years the Israeli military said it is reviewing after being accused of harm.

blocks.text: ByMerlyn ThomasBBC Verify correspondent and Maryam Ahmed

BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome.

Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded.

BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible.

Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them.

Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children.

For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case.

A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range.
How does the IDF investigate incidents?
The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers.

A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations.

In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations.

In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation.

The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents", external, had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war.

These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked.
Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify.

In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security".

It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures".

The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service.

Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations.

Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said.

Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own".

"That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality."

Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments.
"[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said.
Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries.

He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations".
Gaza

Since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.

BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years.
Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review.
A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nahida and Samar Anton were killed by Israeli troops in Gaza in December 2023

blocks.text: Image source, Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem
Nahida and Samar Anton were killed by Israeli troops in Gaza in December 2023

BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident".
In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM".
Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review.
Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information."
It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines."
Deadly attack on school building

blocks.caption: Image caption, Palestinians inspect the destruction following the Israeli attack on the Al-Taba'een school building in August 2024

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Palestinians inspect the destruction following the Israeli attack on the Al-Taba'een school building in August 2024
One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024.
The Hamas-run civil defence agency said at least 93 people, including six women and 11 children, were killed in the strike on the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque.

The buildings had been housing displaced Palestinians when multiple Israeli strikes hit the area at the time of dawn prayers. Videos verified by the BBC of the aftermath showed a cloud of dust as emergency workers worked their way through small fires, rubble and body parts strewn on the floor. Photos taken in daylight showed blood-soaked floors, debris and people's clothes scattered around.
Experts told BBC Verify munition fragments visible at the scene matched that of a GBU-39 - a precision-guided bomb supplied by the US to the Israeli military.

The IDF at the time said a Hamas command and control centre had been embedded in the school building, and that IDF soldiers killed 31 fighters in the incident. It added that according to an "initial review" the casualty numbers did not align with the information held by the IDF, the precise munitions used and the accuracy of the strike. The IDF told BBC Verify this incident remains under review.
West Bank

blocks.caption: Image caption, Women and girls mourn during the funeral of 16-year-old Palestinian Loujain Musleh in the occupied West Bank in September 2024

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Women and girls mourn during the funeral of 16-year-old Palestinian Loujain Musleh in the occupied West Bank in September 2024

BBC Verify also looked into incidents the IDF said it was investigating in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the territory since the 1967 war and built dozens of settlements there, which is illegal under international law.

More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, external. BBC Verify examined more than 50 IDF investigations into incidents in the territory, at least 26 of which involved women and children being killed or injured.
One of those incidents took place just outside of Jenin in September 2024, when Israeli forces reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation.
Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighbouring house.
The Israeli military said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review.
Lebanon

blocks.caption: Image caption, The aftermarth of an Israeli strike in the town of Almat in November 2024

blocks.text: The aftermarth of an Israeli strike in the town of Almat in November 2024
BBC Verify also found nearly 40 IDF investigations into incidents of harm in Lebanon.

The Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in support of Hamas following the 7 October attacks. Israel has since launched two major invasions into Lebanon, where more than 4,000 people have been killed according to the country's health authorities.

One IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify took place on 10 November 2024. An Israeli strike killed 23 people, including seven children, near the city of Byblos, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Verified footage of the aftermath showed smoke rising between rubble and warped metal strewn across the ground where buildings had been destroyed. The IDF said at the time it had targeted a site where Hezbollah had been operating from and storing weapons, and that the incident was under review.
Long running investigations

Michael Schmitt is a professor of international law at the University of Reading who has previously worked closely with the IDF. He said the Israeli military's legal division is the "gold standard in terms of understanding the law", and added that "every allegation that there was a violation does not necessarily trigger a full-blown investigation".

Schmitt said there can be a number of reasons why the IDF may be unable to publicly reveal the details of an investigation or a decision not to pursue one. "For example, you do not want to reveal operational details or particular rules of engagement because the enemy forces will adapt," he said, adding: "And even if you did pursue an investigation, many elements of [it] would remain confidential."
Dill, who is also a co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law and Armed Conflict (ELAC), said: "Three years into this operation, some of these investigations should have been concluded."

She said that when it comes to investigating incidents of harm, "Israel has relied heavily on the argument that it is a rule-of-law country to delegitimatise attempts by the international community to investigate".

"If we have cases of documented abuse that either don't get investigated or the investigations get stuck, and we have reasonable grounds to believe that they get kicked into the long grass, then that would undermine the narrative that Israel is fully capable of taking care of providing accountability," she added.
Methodology
BBC Verify gathered 61,000 reports from BBC News and Reuters which mentioned Gaza, the West Bank or Lebanon, published between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026.

We built an AI search engine to look through those reports for incidents where people may have been injured or killed by Israeli forces, and where the IDF said the report was being investigated, or for example "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined".
This identified almost 5,000 reports. Each one was manually checked by BBC Verify reporters, who excluded any which did not meet the criteria above.
This left 1,343 reports of incidents that the IDF said it was looking into. Some of these reports described the same incidents.
We built another AI tool to remove these duplicate reports. It grouped reports into unique incidents based on the publication date, incident date, location, and numbers reported injured or killed.
We then manually checked that each report had been assigned to the correct group, leaving us with 300 unique incidents.
For each of these incidents we then manually checked our records including the incident date, location, and how many people were killed or injured against the original BBC News or Reuters report.

We shared the details of each case with the IDF including the incident date, location, the news report describing the incident, and the IDF's original comment indicating it was looking into the matter. We asked the IDF for comment and the latest status of each case. The IDF did not say whether any of these investigations had concluded in response to the BBC's requests.

For each incident we also looked for statements on the IDF's website suggesting that the investigation had been concluded, using two different AI assisted web search engines. We found evidence that 28 cases were closed based on statements detailing the findings or indicating that no further steps would be taken.

For a further 18 incidents, it was unclear whether the investigation had been concluded. This included cases where the IDF published initial information about the incident without a clear indication it was closed, and cases where the IDF had characterised some or all of the people killed or injured as combatants, in statements on its own website.
This left us with at least 254 incidents of harm the Israeli military had said it was looking into, for which we did not find a public outcome on the IDF's website.
This was not an exhaustive search, and it is likely that there are more investigations into incidents of harm that were not captured in our search.
Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

articles.title: Poland looks to economic heights in a country transformed since Soviet days
articles.summary:
In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living

Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso…

blocks.text: Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades.

For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.

For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.

blocks.caption: Cezary Błaszczyk and Natalia Kasperska at the Varso Tower. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.
“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.

Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.

blocks.caption: The Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose walks on a 500-metre-long tightrope stretched between the Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower on 31 May. Photograph: Sergei Gapon/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.
“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.

Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.

However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped.

For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.

Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.
Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.

On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.

Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe.
“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”

On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.
The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.

Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.

There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.
Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.

For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.
after newsletter promotion

Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.

Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.

“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”

He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support. Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.

“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.
“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”

As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.

There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.
On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.

blocks.caption: Marcin Łukaszewski, Social Media Manager at CD Projekt Red, gives a tour of the company’s headquarters in Warsaw. Photograph: Anna Liminowicz/The Guardian

blocks.text: As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.
Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.
“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”

Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”

Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.
“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.
“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”

articles.title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region
articles.summary:
Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra

As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke…

blocks.text: As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.

Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.

“This trial of dry ice dispersal is being conducted under the president’s direct instruction to help tackle the haze in South Sumatra,” minister Dudung Abdurachman, was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
“We will first observe the results, and if effective, there is a possibility that this method could be implemented in other regions.”

Since January, almost 900,000 hectares have been burned Indonesia-wide in the worst fire season in more than a decade, exacerbated by this year’s “godzilla” El-Nino and as the practice of “slash and burn” to clear land for crops such as palm oil persists.

blocks.caption: Motorists ride through thick haze from wildfires in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia. Photograph: GENDES/EPA

blocks.text: For months, millions of Indonesians have been subject to thick smoke and an apocalyptic tangerine haze, with criticism mounting of the government’s response, including a class action lawsuit filed last week accusing it of “gross negligence”. Tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to the haze.
Air quality has also plummeted in neighbouring countries, shuttering schools, grounding flights and driving a spike in respiratory illness.

blocks.caption: Marina Bay, Singapore, before and after smoke haze caused by fires in Indonesia.

blocks.text: The haze has drifted into neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and as far afield as the Philippines. Timor-Leste has said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday and urged families to keep children indoors or to use “respiratory protection” if going outside.

Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment starting on Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes occurred. The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents.
In the past week, the financial hub of Singapore was listed among the most polluted cities globally. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected, was at number two.

blocks.caption: Kuala Lumpur’s skyline shrouded in haze from regional wildfires, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on 9 October. Photograph: Hasnoor Hussain/Reuters

blocks.text: On Thursday, a Cessna aircraft will reportedly disperse 1.5 tons of dry ice over the South Sumatran city of Palembang, a move the government hopes will ease the smoke and improve air quality and visibility.
The technique was first deployed in the 1940s to promote ice formation in clouds, Bloomberg reported.
But experts say the use of dry ice, or solid carbon dioxide, might only offer local, and limited relief.
“It’s got some potential for local relief that might work for a while,” says Rick McRae, an adjunct professor from the University of New South Wales’ (UNSW) bushfire research group.

blocks.caption: A pedestrian wearing a mask walks along the boulevard at Marina Bay in Singapore this week. Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Weather systems are all moving from east to west. So if you’re in a town under that and you clear the smoke, there’s gonna be more blowing all the time,” he says, “So it’s a constant … It’s not going to be simple and it’s not going to be a permanent fix in any way.”
In the Indonesian province of central Kalimantan ​on Wednesday, the ISPU air pollution index exceeded 1,200 – or four times the “hazardous” level of 300 – environment ministry data showed.
Local news footage showed ​thick haze blanketing the provincial city of Palangka Raya, cutting visibility for motorists to a minimum.

blocks.caption: Thick wildfire haze shrouds the Kahayan River in Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan, Indonesia. Photograph: GENDES/EPA

blocks.text: Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto has ordered firefighting efforts to be stepped up, and called for a crackdown on those suspected of starting fires.
But the government has struggled to combat the fires, the worst of occur in peatland areas, which can burn for weeks underground and are difficult to extinguish.

“As time goes by and climate change kicks in, I think it could become a global problem, not just the fix that one country needs to find,” said McRae, of the widening regional issue. “There’s a lot of interconnectedness on a global scale.”

articles.title: Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
articles.summary: The alleged victim, who was in a relationship with the woman, had spotted bright green pellets in the meal.

blocks.text: An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison.
Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea.
But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it.

The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November.
Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept.
After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance.
Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death.
"We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network.

articles.title: Victoria to become first state to make abortions free as Coalition matches Labor election promise
articles.summary: Exclusive: Out-of-pocket costs for abortion care to be covered regardless of who wins November election as Jess Wilson says Liberals and Nationals ‘will not allow Labor to play…

blocks.text: Victoria will become the first state in Australia to make access to abortion care free, no matter who wins the November election, with the Coalition matching Labor’s promise just hours after it was announced as it attempts to neutralise the issue.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, on Thursday afternoon told Guardian Australia a Liberal National Coalition government would match Labor’s commitment to cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care up to 16 weeks’ gestation. This would include GP and specialist consultations, scans, tests or medication, which can quickly add up to more than $1,000.

The commitment means Victoria will become the first state in Australia to offer free universal access to abortion services, following the Australian Capital Territory which began covering out-of-pocket costs in 2023.

The Coalition would also expand the Victorian patient transport assistance scheme so that women in regional Victoria who must travel long distances for abortion care would also be eligible for subsidised travel and accommodation.
“The Liberals and Nationals will not allow Labor to play politics on this issue,” Wilson said.
“Labor has had 12 years to improve access to healthcare but are instead choosing to play politics.”

However, the Victorian opposition would not match Labor’s commitment to extend access to medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation or its plan to commission a clinical review into whether it could safely be offered at up to 12 weeks’ gestation.
Currently, medical abortion is subsidised through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for use up to nine weeks but the World Health Organization’s guidance allows for up to 12.
“Only Labor will protect a woman’s right to choose,” Labor’s health minister, Ingrid Stitt, said when she announced the election commitment on Thursday morning.

Stitt’s statement suggested that One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament. It read: “Polling shows the Liberals and One Nation can only form a government together. And One Nation wants to make abortion a criminal offence.”
However, Wilson on Thursday again ruled out changes to abortion laws under a Coalition government.
after newsletter promotion

“Victorians know where I stand on this issue. There will be no changes to abortion laws under a government I lead. Full stop. And I think it’s incredibly disappointing to see Labor playing politics with women’s reproductive rights five minutes before an election,” she said.
Wilson has previously described abortion as a personal decision that should be made by women in consultation with healthcare professionals.
The premier, Ben Carroll, earlier on Thursday said Labor “decriminalised abortion and we will stand up for it” as he warned that One Nation posed a threat.

“Let’s be very clear: you’ve seen the leader of One Nation very clearly say that he wants to roll back access to abortion. He wants to rob women of their right to choose their own future,” Carroll told reporters.
Abortion was decriminalised in Victoria in 2008, with women able to obtain a termination during the first 24 weeks of pregnancy, and later if they obtain the agreement of two doctors.

articles.title: Brazil to shorten workweek in win for Lula ahead of runoff
articles.summary: Brazil's Senate approved cutting the workweek from 44 to 40 hours. The move could give President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva an edge over his opponent, Flavio Bolsonaro, ahead of the October 25 runoff.

image.caption: Amendment lowers working hours from 44 hours a week to 40, providing Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva a key legislative win ahead of Oct. 25 runoff [Photo: October 11]Image: Paulo Lopes/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Brazil's Senate on Thursday approved a constitutional amendment to reduce the working week to five days from six without a salary cut, likely providing President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva with an edge ahead of Flavio Bolsonaro in the presidential runoff on October 25.
Lula is expected to sign the shorter workweek into law next week.

Brazil's leftist leader has taken a number of steps in recent days to shore up support before the runoff, including new fuel tax cuts, extending existing subsidies and pledging to pardon the debts of more than 3.6 million small businesses to the federal government and others.
But the pledge to trim the workweek turned into a top promise that Lula hoped to deliver on before the runoff.
Brazil election: Lula faces Flavio Bolsonaro in runoff
"6x1" reform receives overwhelming support
The new amendment, known as the "6x1" reform, could benefit more than 37 million workers, according to the government.
"The end of the 6x1 is more than a change in the workday. It's more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow, take care of yourself, and enjoy life," Lula wrote on X.
"Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve time to live. It's a victory for workers. It's Brazil ready for more," he said.
But the legislation still leaves out a large number of people in the shadow economy, like freelancers and delivery drivers.
Lula, a former trade unionist, worked on the proposal to reduce the workweek with his government over the course of the year.
Bolsonaro backs "6x1" reform after opposing it

Flavio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator and the eldest son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, had long opposed the legislation. But Flavio Bolsonaro reversed course on Tuesday to say that he'll back the bill because it has so much support.

Many businesses opposed the bill because it would raise their costs, and Bolsonaro previously argued for estabilishing a flexible payment regime where individuals negotiate their pay with their employers.
He repeatedly called the legislation election-motivated.
In the first round of elections earlier this month, Bolsonaro dealt Lula a bruising defeat, finishing ahead with 47% of the vote, though short of the 50% needed for an outright majority.
The campaign in Brazil has been dominated by voter frustration over high street crime, the strength of Evangelical churches, the high tax burden for businesses and economic dissatisfaction.

articles.title: El Niño damage to agriculture hits P6.8 billion
articles.summary: Agricultural damage has reached P6.8 billion this year as several areas struggle with dry spells linked to the very strong El Niño phenomenon in recent months.

blocks.text: October 15, 2026 | 11:13am
Farm workers check on their crops, spray organic pesticides, and remove unwanted weeds at a rice field in Tanay, Rizal on Sept. 19, 2023.
Ernie Penaredondo

MANILA, Philippines — Agricultural damage has reached P6.8 billion this year as several areas struggle with dry spells linked to the very strong El Niño phenomenon in recent months, according to the Office of Civil Defense (OCD).

OCD spokesperson Junie Castillo said on Thursday, October 15, that while the amount accounts for the total damage recorded this year, the reduced water supply for irrigation due to lower rainfall has negatively affected crop production in some areas over the past two months.

“May mga nakaranas na nung dry spells at drought. Ibig sabihin, mga two months na bawas na sa mga pag-ulan, kaya ‘yung mga patubig sa mga agrikultura, kaya nagkaroon na rin ng kabawasan sa produksyon ng iba’t ibang crops sa iba’t ibang lugar,” Castillo said in an interview with dzMM.

(Some areas have already experienced dry spells and drought. That means rainfall has been reduced for the past two months, and so has irrigation for agriculture, resulting in a decline in the production of different crops across different areas.)

The agency added that, as of press time, 109 areas had already declared a state of calamity due to the impacts of El Niño, with most local government units expressing concerns over agricultural damage.
Concerns on rice, vegetable supplies

The Philippine Chamber of Agriculture and Food Inc., a private-sector group focused on agribusiness and food security, has also expressed concerns about the impacts of El Niño on the agriculture sector, including vegetable and rice supplies.

The group’s president, Danilo Fausto, said on Thursday, October 15, in a separate interview with dzRH that the rice supply of the National Food Authority (NFA) is currently insufficient and may last only 51 days, instead of the ideal 70 to 90 days.

He also warned that several factors, including the depreciation of the peso, rising importation costs, and the impact of El Niño on other countries from which the Philippines usually imports rice, may drive up domestic rice prices.

Fausto also said that while vegetable production is currently in favorable condition and is expected to remain so until the end of 2026, harvests may decline by the first quarter of next year as dry conditions worsen.

“We are expecting this last quarter meron tayong mga gulay…kasi maganda ang harvest natin. Ang problema pagdating mo next year ng first quarter towards March tuyot na ‘yan so hindi masyadong lalaki ang mga gulay,” Fausto said.

(We are expecting this last quarter that we will have vegetables… because our harvests are good. The problem is when drought comes in the first quarter towards March next year, the vegetables may no longer grow properly.)
Gov’t interventions

The OCD said the government has provided about P10 billion worth of assistance, particularly through the Department of Agriculture (DA), to help farmers prepare for the anticipated worsening dry conditions.
According to Castillo, the assistance included the distribution of water pumps, seeds and fertilizers, as well as livelihood support programs.

He also mentioned that the government has a National Action Plan for El Niño to monitor and address the situation in the areas of food security, water security, health security, energy and public safety during the phenomenon.

The state weather bureau PAGASA had earlier reported that drought may affect all provinces in the country in March 2027, warning the public of potential El Niño risks such as water shortages and heat-related illnesses.

US dollar and Philippine peso bills are seen in this file photo.
Philstar.com / File photo
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine peso breached the P63:$1 level for the first time on Thursday, hitting a fresh record low against the US dollar amid renewed tensions in the Middle East.
Data from the Bankers Association of the Philippines showed the peso weakened to P63.15:$1 in early trading, surpassing its previous intraday record low of P62.925.
The peso opened at P62.83:$1 before closing at P62.87:$1 on Wednesday, October 14.
The previous close was just three centavos shy of the record-low closing rate of P62.90 recorded on October 8.

articles.title: White House defends new press secretary amid questions about her legal credentials
articles.summary: Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived.

blocks.text: The White House is defending its new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, as she faces scrutiny over her legal credentials.
President Donald Trump described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment last week and she has referred to herself as a lawyer.
But when she was asked on Tuesday by a reporter in which state she had passed the bar exam required to be an attorney in the US, she said standing alongside the president: "When I moved to China."

She does not appear to be registered to the bar in any state where she has lived. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia is "uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people".
Responding to questions about her credentials, Zacharia said in a statement this week: "I practised international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."
On Wednesday, a watchdog group, Campaign for Accountability, filed a complaint with the California State Bar Association.
They are seeking an investigation into whether Zacharia "repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practise law without a licence to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime".
The 42-year-old political strategist graduated from law school at Pepperdine University in California in 2011, the university confirmed.
A law degree is not a licence to practise law in the US.
The new White House press secretary told the New York Times on Wednesday that when she first began appearing on cable news, she had asked Pepperdine how she should identify herself.
She said she was advised by the university president that she could call herself a lawyer, but not an attorney.

Zacharia took the bar exam in California after graduating from law school but did not pass, according to the Wall Street Journal. California's bar exam is widely regarded as one of the hardest in the US to pass.
A person with direct knowledge of the matter told the outlet that Zacharia took the exam around the same time that she was planning a wedding and preparing to move to China with her husband-to-be.
She moved to Beijing because of her husband's job at an American private equity firm. Zacharia has said she worked on "international transaction law" there.
Her LinkedIn profile states that she worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011-13.
In China, only Chinese citizens are eligible to obtain a licence to practise law. Foreign employees may work at law firms in other roles.

In February last year, Zacharia said on conservative radio programme The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show that she had worked as outside counsel for the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the World Bank during her time in China.
The BBC has contacted the World Bank and IFC for comment.
It is understood the World Bank Group sometimes retains outside law firms, and that those firms decide which of their lawyers are assigned to which parts of any work.
Zacharia has also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally Ric Grenell, according to her LinkedIn profile.
